title: Ecclesiastes - Introduction
content:
Introduction to Ecclesiastes

Outline of Ecclesiastes

  1. The author questions the nature of life and the limits of human wisdom (1:1–6:12).
  2. The author teaches about making wise choices in how one lives (7:1–12:7)
  3. The conclusion and ending (12:8–14)

What is the book of Ecclesiastes about?

Ecclesiastes is a group of short teachings that try to answer questions such as “What profit {belongs} to humanity in exchange for all his toil that he toils under the sun?” (1:3) Ecclesiastes is a series of thoughts about a variety of subjects, all of them about the purpose and worth of various actions and events. The author concludes that all the work we perform and all the knowledge and skill we gain are as a vapor that disappears, and that we must fear Yahweh and keep his commandments.

How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title for this book is “Ecclesiastes.” Its meaning is similar to “religious assembly.” Translators might use a different title such as “Words of a Teacher” or “Teachings of a Wise Man.”

Who wrote the book of Ecclesiastes?

The writer calls himself Qoheleth and identifies himself as “the son of David, king in Jerusalem.” Jewish and Christian tradition identify Qoheleth with King Solomon based on:

  • his wisdom (1:16 and twenty-six other references to wisdom)
  • his vast wealth (2:8) and the pain that comes from wealth (4:8, 5:13–14, 9:11)
  • his large number of servants (2:7 and 10:7)
  • his limitless opportunities for worldly pleasures (2:1–2, 9, 3:13, 4:8, 5:4 and 12:1) and
  • the wide range of his many building projects (2:4–6).

Some scholars think that Qoheleth was a later anonymous Jewish writer. He appears to have written the book of Ecclesiastes near the end of his life, as he reflected on what he gained from all that he did.

Why are there so many apparent contradictions in the book of Ecclesiastes?

Some scholars think the author was a faithful man. Other scholars think that the author made bad decisions and was sorrowful when he wrote this book. Apparent contradictions in the book may indicate that Qoheleth’s faith was sometimes weak. Or it is also possible that the teachings in the book differ from each other in order to relate to different things happening in the lives of readers.

Religious and Cultural Concepts

What does this book teach about how God repays people?

In the ancient Near East, people were concerned with why they were being punished or blessed. They often connected these things to their gods. The writer of Ecclesiastes explains that Yahweh will bless and reward people for the right things they do and punish people for the evil things they do. But this might not happen in this life.

What value did the Israelites place on the book of Ecclesiastes?

The Israelites have often questioned the value of this book. This is due in large part to its unusual wording and teachings. At times, it appears to disagree with the rest of Scripture. While many have questioned its authority, it has been affirmed to be Scripture. It gives valuable lessons concerning the uselessness of pursuing any goal other than to give Yahweh glory.

Vapor as Futility

The Hebrew word translated as “vapor” recurs as a thematic refrain throughout Ecclesiastes, declaring human achievements fleeting. It indicates transience, not moral worthlessness. The paired phrase “pursuit of wind” intensifies this assessment.

Translation Issues

What is the meaning of “under the sun?”

“Under the sun” here is another way of saying “on the earth.” When the author says that there is “nothing new under the sun,” this means that every kind of thing has already happened before on the earth. While a particular event may not have specifically occurred before, something similar has already occurred. Translate this phrase consistently through the book.

How do I translate harsh or shocking passages?

Parts of the book of Ecclesiastes can be shocking or surprising to read in Scripture. For example, “If a man should father a hundred {children}, and many years should he live—and many that the days of his years may be—but {if} his soul is not satisfied from the good {thing} (and also a burial place is not for him), I say, ‘Better than him {is} the stillborn child.’” (6:3). The translator should allow these difficulties to remain and not try to make them less surprising.

How is life described in the book of Ecclesiastes?

The author of Ecclesiastes concludes that everything in this life quickly passes away, like a vapor that disappears. A person’s circumstances or character and even all of the things of this world have little or no significance apart from God. That is because God gives meaning to everything.

At the end of their life, people often say that the years of their life seemed short. The author of Ecclesiastes used the metaphor of vapor or breath to describe how life ends while it seems to be just beginning.

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 1 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 1 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

The chapter opens with a title (1), a poem on the endless cycles of nature (2–11), and Qoheleth’s first-person search for wisdom (12–18).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial. For a more thorough discussion of this, see the Introduction to Ecclesiastes.

Under the sun

This recurring idiom means “in this life” or “on the earth.” See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for a more thorough explanation of this phrase.

title: Ecclesiastes 1:1 (#1)
content:
קֹהֶ֣לֶת

"Qoheleth"

The word Qoheleth is the name that the main speaker of this book chose to use for himself. In the original language it is a title that means “one who assembles a group,” that is, someone who gathers people together in order to teach them. You could spell out how this name sounds in your language, as the ULT does, or you could translate its meaning.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Ecclesiastes 1:2 (#1)
content:
הֲבֵ֤ל הֲבָלִים֙

"Vapor of vapors"

Qoheleth is using Vapor of vapors as a common expression of his culture to mean “the most fleeting thing of all.” In this expression, a word is repeated in the possessive form in order to express a superlative. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The most fleeting thing of all] or [Utterly temporary]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:2 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠כֹּ֥ל הָֽבֶל

"the whole {is} vapor"

Qoheleth says the whole as an extreme statement for emphasis. He does not mean that every single thing without exception is fleeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [just about everything is vapor]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 1:3 (#1)
content:
מַה־יִּתְר֖וֹן לָֽ⁠אָדָ֑ם בְּ⁠כָל־עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ שֶֽׁ⁠יַּעֲמֹ֖ל תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"What profit {belongs} to humanity in exchange for all his toil that he toils under the sun"

Qoheleth is not using the question form to emphasize that people gain nothing lasting from all their labor. Instead, this is a genuine question. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wonder if there is any profit for a human in exchange for all his toil that he toils under the sun!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 1:3 (#2)
content:
יִּתְר֖וֹן

"profit"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of profit, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [good thing that lasts]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 1:3 (#3)
content:
עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ שֶֽׁ⁠יַּעֲמֹ֖ל

"his toil that he toils"

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Ecclesiastes 1:3 (#4)
content:
תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"under the sun"

Qoheleth is using under the sun as a common expression of his culture to mean “in this life on the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for more information on translating this expression here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [in this earthly life]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:4 (#1)
content:
דּ֤וֹר הֹלֵךְ֙ וְ⁠ד֣וֹר בָּ֔א

"A generation is going and a generation is coming"

Qoheleth is referring to the whole cycle of human life by naming its two major components, one generation going and another generation coming. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People are continually dying and being born]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 1:5 (#1)
content:
שׁוֹאֵ֛ף זוֹרֵ֥חַֽ ה֖וּא שָֽׁם

"panting, it is rising there"

Qoheleth is speaking of the sun as if it were a living thing that could be panting as it hurried back to the place where it rises. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it goes back quickly to rise there again]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 1:6 (#1)
content:
אֶל־דָּר֔וֹם וְ⁠סוֹבֵ֖ב אֶל־צָפ֑וֹן

"to {the} south and turning to {the} north"

Qoheleth is referring to all directions by naming two major components, south and north. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in every direction]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 1:6 (#2)
content:
הוֹלֵ֣ךְ הָ⁠ר֔וּחַ וְ⁠עַל־סְבִיבֹתָ֖י⁠ו שָׁ֥ב הָ⁠רֽוּחַ

"the wind is going; and on its courses, the wind is returning"

Qoheleth is speaking of the wind as if it were a living thing that could choose where to travel and then decide to return the same way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the wind simply blows around and around in the same course]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 1:8 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־תִמָּלֵ֥א אֹ֖זֶן

"and an ear is not filled"

The expression is not filled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and an ear does not fill up]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 1:8 (#2)
content:
כָּל־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים יְגֵעִ֔ים

"All the things {are} wearisome"

Qoheleth says All the things are wearisome and a person is not able to speak as extreme statements for emphasis. He means that the endless repetition he has been describing is exhausting to consider and that no one could ever finish describing how wearisome these things are. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Very many things indeed are wearisome; a person could never finish describing them]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 1:8 (#3)
content:
אִ֖ישׁ

"a person"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 1:8 (#4)
content:
לֹא־תִשְׂבַּ֥ע עַ֨יִן֙ לִ⁠רְא֔וֹת וְ⁠לֹא־תִמָּלֵ֥א אֹ֖זֶן מִ⁠שְּׁמֹֽעַ

"An eye is not satisfied of seeing, and an ear is not filled from hearing"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [People are never satisfied by anything they see or hear]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 1:9 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מַה־שֶׁ⁠נַּֽעֲשָׂ֔ה ה֖וּא שֶׁ⁠יֵּעָשֶׂ֑ה

"and whatever that which has been done, it {is} that which will be done"

The expressions has been done and will be done are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and whatever people have done, it that which people will do]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 1:9 (#2)
content:
תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"under the sun"

See how you translated the same expression in 1:3.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:10 (#1)
content:
יֵ֥שׁ דָּבָ֛ר שֶׁ⁠יֹּאמַ֥ר רְאֵה־זֶ֖ה חָדָ֣שׁ ה֑וּא

"Is} there a thing about which one says, “See this, it {is} new"

Qoheleth is using the question form to make an emphatic statement, that nothing anyone points to is actually new. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is nothing about which one says, “See this, it is new!”]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 1:10 (#2)
content:
שֶׁ⁠יֹּאמַ֥ר

"about which one says"

The pronoun one refers to any person at all, not to a specific individual. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [about which anyone says]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 1:10 (#3)
content:
רְאֵה־זֶ֖ה חָדָ֣שׁ ה֑וּא

"See this, it {is} new"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that this thing is something new]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Ecclesiastes 1:10 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠לְּ⁠פָנֵֽ⁠נוּ

"from before our faces"

Here, our faces represents “us,” that is, the people who are alive now. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before us]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 1:11 (#1)
content:
זִכְר֖וֹן

"a memory of"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of memory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anyone remembering]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 1:11 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠רִאשֹׁנִ֑ים וְ⁠גַ֨ם לָ⁠אַחֲרֹנִ֜ים

"the former {times}, and also, of the latter {times"

Qoheleth is referring to people and events of every time by naming two major components, the former times and the latter times. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people and events of every time]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#1)
content:
כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר נַעֲשָׂ֖ה

"all that is done"

The expression is done is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all that people are doing]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַ֣תִּי אֶת־לִבִּ֗⁠י

"So I gave my heart"

Qoheleth is using I gave my heart as a common expression of his culture to mean “I devoted my mind.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So, I set my mind]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠דְר֤וֹשׁ וְ⁠לָ⁠תוּר֙

"to seek and to explore"

The terms to seek and to explore mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis, indicating that his investigation was thorough. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to search out thoroughly]

See: Doublet

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#4)
content:
בַּֽ⁠חָכְמָ֔ה

"with wisdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wisdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wisely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#5)
content:
תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁמָ֑יִם

"under the heavens"

Qoheleth is using under the heavens as a common expression of his culture to mean “in this life on the earth.” This expression means the same thing as “under the sun” in 1:3. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during this earthly life]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#6)
content:
עִנְיַ֣ן רָ֗ע

"an unpleasant business"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of business, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something unpleasant that]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"to the sons of humanity"

Qoheleth is using the sons of humanity as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to human beings]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:14 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠רְע֥וּת רֽוּחַ

"and pursuit of wind"

Qoheleth is speaking of everything people do as if it were a pursuit of wind. He means that gaining anything lasting from these deeds is as futile as trying to catch the wind. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and as futile as trying to catch the wind]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 1:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"and—behold"

Qoheleth is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation here and in verse 16. Alternate translation: [and—pay attention]

See: Foreground Information

title: Ecclesiastes 1:15 (#1)
content:
מְעֻוָּ֖ת לֹא־יוּכַ֣ל לִ⁠תְקֹ֑ן

"A bent {thing}—one is not able to straighten {it"

Qoheleth is speaking of what is wrong in the world as if it were a bent object that someone might try to make straight. He means that people cannot correct the things that are wrong with life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is wrong in life—no one is able to make it right]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 (#1)
content:
דִּבַּ֨רְתִּי אֲנִ֤י עִם־לִבִּ⁠י֙

"I spoke, I, with my heart"

See how you translated the phrase my heart in 1:13

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר

"saying"

The word saying introduces the words that Qoheleth spoke to himself. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠פָנַ֖⁠י עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם

"before my face over Jerusalem"

Here, my face represents Qoheleth speaking of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before me in Jerusalem]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לִבִּ֛⁠י רָאָ֥ה הַרְבֵּ֖ה חָכְמָ֥ה וָ⁠דָֽעַת

"and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge"

Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a person who could see. In this culture, the heart represented a person’s thoughts and understanding, and seeing something represented experiencing and knowing it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in my thinking I have experienced much wisdom and knowledge]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 (#5)
content:
חָכְמָ֥ה וָ⁠דָֽעַת

"wisdom and knowledge"

The terms wisdom and knowledge mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [wise understanding]

See: Doublet

title: Ecclesiastes 1:17 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤⁠ה לִבִּ⁠י֙

"So, I gave my heart"

See how you translated the same expression in 1:13.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 1:17 (#2)
content:
חָכְמָ֔ה וְ⁠דַ֥עַת הוֹלֵל֖וֹת וְ⁠שִׂכְל֑וּת

"wisdom and to know madness and folly"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of wisdom, madness, and folly, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what is sound judgment and what is poor judgment]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 1:17 (#3)
content:
רַעְי֥וֹן רֽוּחַ

"pursuit of wind"

See how you translated the same expression in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 1:18 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב חָכְמָ֖ה רָב־כָּ֑עַס וְ⁠יוֹסִ֥יף דַּ֖עַת יוֹסִ֥יף מַכְאֽוֹב

"in much wisdom {is} much anger, and {when} one increases knowledge, he increases pain"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of wisdom, anger, knowledge, and pain, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [For in much wise thinking is much angry feeling, and when one increases the things he knows, he increases the things that hurt him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 2 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 2 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Qoheleth narrates a first-person experiment: he tests pleasure (1–11), weighs wisdom against folly (12–23), and concludes that enjoying food, drink, and work is God’s gift (24–26).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vapor

See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for a discussion of this term.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

The Heart

Qoheleth speaks with and to his “heart,” in Hebrew the seat of thinking and deciding rather than of emotion.

Under the sun

See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for a discussion of this phrase.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:1 (#1)
content:
אָמַ֤רְתִּֽי אֲנִי֙ בְּ⁠לִבִּ֔⁠י

"I spoke, I with my heart"

Qoheleth is speaking of his own thoughts as if they were a person that he could talk to, his heart. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I thought to myself]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:1 (#2)
content:
בְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֖ה וּ⁠רְאֵ֣ה בְ⁠ט֑וֹב

"with joy and see good"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of joy, you could express that idea in another way. Also, Qoheleth is speaking of good as if it were a thing that he could see. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by making you glad and letting you experience what is pleasant]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:1 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"But behold"

Qoheleth is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. See how you translated this word in 1:14.

See: Foreground Information

title: Ecclesiastes 2:1 (#4)
content:
גַם־ה֖וּא הָֽבֶל

"it also {was} vapor"

See how you translated this word in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:2 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠שְׂח֖וֹק אָמַ֣רְתִּי מְהוֹלָ֑ל וּ⁠לְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֖ה

"To laughter I said, “Madness!” And to joy"

Qoheleth is speaking To laughter and to joy though he knows they cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening that he feels very strongly about these emotions and their place in life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about them. Alternate translation: [About laughter, I said, “Madness!” And about joy]

See: Apostrophe

title: Ecclesiastes 2:2 (#2)
content:
מְהוֹלָ֑ל

"Madness"

Qoheleth is using a word that expresses a strong feeling of scorn. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Ridiculous]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 2:2 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֖ה מַה־זֹּ֥ה עֹשָֽׂה

"And to joy, “What is this doing"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And to joy, I said, “What is this doing]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 2:2 (#4)
content:
מַה־זֹּ֥ה עֹשָֽׂה

"What is this doing"

Qoheleth is using the question form to show that pleasure accomplishes nothing worthwhile. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This accomplishes nothing!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠מְשׁ֥וֹךְ בַּ⁠יַּ֖יִן אֶת־בְּשָׂרִ֑⁠י

"to drag my flesh with wine"

Qoheleth is using to drag my flesh with wine as a common expression of the culture to mean “to gratify my body with wine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to gratify my body with wine]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לִבִּ֞⁠י נֹהֵ֤ג בַּֽ⁠חָכְמָה֙

"and my heart was guiding {me} with wisdom"

Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a living thing that could guide him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I was still thinking wisely all the while]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֶ⁠אֱחֹ֣ז בְּ⁠סִכְל֔וּת

"and to seize folly"

Qoheleth is speaking of folly as if it were an object that he could take hold of with his hand. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to take up foolish behavior]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 (#4)
content:
ט֜וֹב לִ⁠בְנֵ֤י הָ⁠אָדָם֙

"is the} good for the sons of humanity"

Here the masculine term sons has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. See how you translated the same phrase in 1:13.

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 (#5)
content:
תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם

"under the heavens"

Qoheleth is using under the heavens as a common expression of the culture to mean “here on the earth during this life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:3. Alternate translation: [here on the earth]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 2:4 (#1)
content:
בָּנִ֤יתִי לִ⁠י֙ בָּתִּ֔ים נָטַ֥עְתִּי לִ֖⁠י כְּרָמִֽים

"I built for myself houses. I planted for myself vineyards"

Qoheleth is using I built for myself houses and I planted for myself vineyards to represent the work that he had others do for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I had houses built for myself. I had vineyards planted for myself]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 2:5 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠פַרְדֵּסִ֑ים

"and royal parks"

The term royal parks describes large, enclosed gardens that belonged to a king. If your readers would not be familiar with what royal parks are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and large walled gardens]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:5 (#2)
content:
עֵ֥ץ כָּל־פֶּֽרִי

"a tree of each fruit"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe a tree that is characterized by the kind of fruit that it bears. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [every kind of fruit tree]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 2:7 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְנֵי־בַ֖יִת

"and sons of the house"

Qoheleth is using sons of the house as a common expression of the culture to mean “servants who were born in my household.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and servants born in my household]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 2:7 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠פָנַ֖⁠י

"to my face"

Here the expression to my face means “before me” (in time). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [before me]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 2:8 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠סְגֻלַּ֥ת מְלָכִ֖ים וְ⁠הַ⁠מְּדִינ֑וֹת

"and the treasure of kings and provinces"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe treasure that is characterized by belonging to kings and provinces. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the treasure that kings and provinces possessed]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 2:8 (#2)
content:
שִׁדָּ֥ה וְ⁠שִׁדּֽוֹת

"breast and breasts"

Qoheleth is using breast and breasts to represent women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an abundance of women] or [many women for myself]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 2:9 (#1)
content:
חָכְמָתִ֖⁠י עָ֥מְדָה לִּֽ⁠י

"my wisdom stood by me"

Qoheleth is speaking of his wisdom as if it were a living thing that could stand beside him as a companion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I remained wise through it all]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 2:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠זֶֽה־הָיָ֥ה חֶלְקִ֖⁠י מִ⁠כָּל־עֲמָלִֽ⁠י

"and this was my portion from all my toil"

Qoheleth is speaking of the enjoyment that he received from his work as if it were a portion of land or food that had been assigned to him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and this was what I received in return for all my toil]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:11 (#1)
content:
שֶֽׁ⁠עָשׂ֣וּ יָדַ֔⁠י

"that my hands had done"

Here, my hands represents my own efforts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that I had accomplished by my own efforts]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 2:11 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בֶֽ⁠עָמָ֖ל שֶׁ⁠עָמַ֣לְתִּי לַ⁠עֲשׂ֑וֹת

"and to {the} toil that I toiled to do"

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of expressing this. Alternate translation: [and to the work that I had labored to accomplish]

See: Poetry

title: Ecclesiastes 2:11 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠רְע֣וּת ר֔וּחַ

"and pursuit of wind"

See how you translated the same expression in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֥ין יִתְר֖וֹן תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"and there was no profit under the sun"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of profit, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and nothing under the sun benefited me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:12 (#1)
content:
מֶ֣ה הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם שֶׁ⁠יָּבוֹא֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר־כְּבָ֖ר עָשֽׂוּ⁠הוּ

"what {can} the person {do} who will come after the king {than} that which he has already done"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that whoever comes after him will not be able to do anything more than what has already been done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [the person who will come after the king can do nothing more than what has already been done.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:12 (#2)
content:
מֶ֣ה הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם שֶׁ⁠יָּבוֹא֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ

"what {can} the person {do} who will come after the king"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person. He means people in general who might come after him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what can any person do who will come after the king]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 2:12 (#3)
content:
אַחֲרֵ֣י הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ

"after the king"

Qoheleth is speaking of himself in the third person as the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [after me]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Ecclesiastes 2:13 (#1)
content:
כִּֽ⁠יתְר֥וֹן הָ⁠א֖וֹר מִן־הַ⁠חֹֽשֶׁךְ

"as {there is} a profit of the light more than the darkness"

The point of this comparison is that just as the light is more useful than the darkness for seeing where one is going, so wisdom is more useful than folly for living well. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as light helps a person to see where he is going, but darkness does not]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 2:14 (#1)
content:
הֶֽ⁠חָכָם֙ עֵינָ֣י⁠ו בְּ⁠רֹאשׁ֔⁠וֹ

"The wise, his eyes {are} in his head"

Qoheleth is using the expression that his eyes are in his head as a common expression of the culture to mean “he sees where he is going.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The wise, he sees where he is going]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 2:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠כְּסִ֖יל בַּ⁠חֹ֣שֶׁךְ הוֹלֵ֑ךְ

"but the fool in the darkness is walking"

Qoheleth is speaking of the way a foolish person lives as if it were walking in the darkness. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the fool lives without understanding]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:14 (#3)
content:
שֶׁ⁠מִּקְרֶ֥ה אֶחָ֖ד יִקְרֶ֥ה אֶת־כֻּלָּֽ⁠ם

"that one happening will happen to both of them"

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its subject come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. The implication is that the one happening that will happen to both of them is death. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternatively, your language may have another way of expressing this. Alternate translation: [that the same thing will occur to both of them] or [that one thing, namely death, will happen to both of them]

See: Poetry

title: Ecclesiastes 2:15 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠מִקְרֵ֤ה הַ⁠כְּסִיל֙ גַּם־אֲנִ֣י יִקְרֵ֔⁠נִי

"As {the} happening of the fool, even {to} me—it will happen {to} me"

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas, the very thing that happens to the fool will happen to me too]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 2:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לָ֧⁠מָּה חָכַ֛מְתִּי אֲנִ֖י אָ֣ז יוֹתֵ֑ר

"And why was I, I, wise then, abundantly"

Qoheleth is using the question form to express his frustration that becoming wise gained him no lasting advantage. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And so I was exceedingly wise for no reason at all!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠דִבַּ֣רְתִּי בְ⁠לִבִּ֔⁠י שֶׁ⁠גַּם־זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל

"And I said to my heart that also this {is} vapor"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [And I said to my heart, “This also is vapor.”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Ecclesiastes 2:16 (#1)
content:
אֵ֨ין זִכְר֧וֹן לֶ⁠חָכָ֛ם

"there is no memory of the wise {person"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of memory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people do not remember the wise person]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:16 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠כֹּ֣ל נִשְׁכָּ֔ח

"both {will be} forgotten"

The expression forgotten is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one will remember either of them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 2:16 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֛יךְ יָמ֥וּת הֶ⁠חָכָ֖ם עִֽם־הַ⁠כְּסִֽיל

"Alas! The wise die with the fool"

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible! The wise die with the fool]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 2:17 (#1)
content:
הַֽ⁠מַּעֲשֶׂ֔ה שֶׁ⁠נַּעֲשָׂ֖ה תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"was} the work that was done under the sun"

The expression was done is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [was the work that people did under the sun]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 2:18 (#1)
content:
אֶת־כָּל־עֲמָלִ֔⁠י שֶׁ⁠אֲנִ֥י עָמֵ֖ל תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"all my toil that I had toiled under the sun"

Here, my toil represents what I had gained by my toil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the possessions that I had earned by my hard work under the sun]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 2:19 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֣י יוֹדֵ֗עַ הֶֽ⁠חָכָ֤ם יִהְיֶה֙ א֣וֹ סָכָ֔ל

"And who knows: Will he be wise or a fool"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to know the answer. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And no one knows whether he will be wise or a fool.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:19 (#2)
content:
הֶֽ⁠חָכָ֤ם יִהְיֶה֙ א֣וֹ סָכָ֔ל

"Will he be wise or a fool"

The pronoun he refers to the person who will come after Qoheleth, whom he mentions at the end of the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Will that person who comes after me be wise or a fool]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 2:19 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יִשְׁלַט֙ בְּ⁠כָל־עֲמָלִ֔⁠י

"And he will have authority over all my toil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of authority, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And he will rule over all my toil]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:21 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠חָכְמָ֥ה וּ⁠בְ⁠דַ֖עַת וּ⁠בְ⁠כִשְׁר֑וֹן

"is} with wisdom and with knowledge and with skill"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of wisdom and knowledge and skill, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [is that of someone who is wise, knows much, and who possesses skills]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:22 (#1)
content:
כִּ֠י מֶֽה־הֹוֶ֤ה לָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ בְּ⁠כָל־עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠בְ⁠רַעְי֖וֹן לִבּ֑⁠ו שֶׁ⁠ה֥וּא עָמֵ֖ל תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"For what endures for the person in exchange for all his toil and in the striving of his heart {in} which he {is} a toiler under the sun"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that nothing lasting comes to a person from all his hard work. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For nothing endures for the person in exchange for all his toil and the striving of his heart with which he labors under the sun.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:23 (#1)
content:
כָל־יָמָ֣י⁠ו מַכְאֹבִ֗ים וָ⁠כַ֨עַס֙ עִנְיָנ֔⁠וֹ

"all his days {are} pains, and anger {is} his business"

Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s days as if they were pains and of his anger as if it were business. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all his days are full of pain, and his work causes him grief]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 2:23 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠כַ֨עַס֙ עִנְיָנ֔⁠וֹ

"and anger {is} his business"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of anger and business, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and he works angrily]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 2:24 (#1)
content:
אֵֽין־ט֤וֹב בָּ⁠אָדָם֙ שֶׁ⁠יֹּאכַ֣ל וְ⁠שָׁתָ֔ה

"There is nothing better for humanity {than} that he should eat and drink"

Here the masculine term he has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [There is nothing better for humanity than that he or she should eat and drink]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Ecclesiastes 2:24 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֶרְאָ֧ה אֶת־נַפְשׁ֛⁠וֹ ט֖וֹב בַּ⁠עֲמָל֑⁠וֹ

"and cause his spirit to see good in his toil"

Qoheleth is using cause his spirit to see good as a common expression of the culture to mean “find enjoyment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and enjoy himself in his toil]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 2:24 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠יַּ֥ד הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֖ים

"is} from the hand of the God"

Here, the hand of the God represents what God gives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is what God gives]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 2:25 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י מִ֥י יֹאכַ֛ל וּ⁠מִ֥י יָח֖וּשׁ ח֥וּץ מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

"for who will eat and who will enjoy apart from him"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to eat or to enjoy anything apart from God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for no one can eat or enjoy anything apart from him!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 2:25 (#2)
content:
ח֥וּץ מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

"apart from him"

Some ancient manuscripts read “apart from him.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “apart from me.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Ecclesiastes 2:26 (#1)
content:
שֶׁ⁠טּ֣וֹב לְ⁠פָנָ֔י⁠ו

"who {is} good to his face"

Here, to his face represents in his judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who is good in his judgment]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 2:26 (#2)
content:
נָתַ֛ן חָכְמָ֥ה וְ⁠דַ֖עַת וְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֑ה

"he gives wisdom and knowledge and joy"

The pronoun he refers to God, whom Qoheleth names later in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 2:26 (#3)
content:
לֶ⁠אֱס֣וֹף וְ⁠לִ⁠כְנ֗וֹס

"of gathering and of collecting"

The terms gathering and collecting mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [of amassing wealth]

See: Doublet

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 3 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 3 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter opens with a poem listing 14 pairs of contrasting activities assigned to appointed times (1–8), then reflects on God’s sovereignty, human limitation, injustice, and the shared mortality of humans and animals (9–22).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Eternity in the human heart

In verse 11, God places eternity in the human heart yet limits understanding of his work, creating a tension central to the chapter’s argument.

content:
תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּׁמָֽיִם

"under the heavens"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:13

title: Ecclesiastes 3:2 (#1)
content:
עֵ֥ת לָ⁠לֶ֖דֶת וְ⁠עֵ֣ת לָ⁠מ֑וּת

"a time to give birth and a time to die"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is a time to give birth and a time to die]

title: Ecclesiastes 3:2 (#2)

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 4 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 4 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Qoheleth moves from observing oppression (1–3) to reflecting on envy-driven labor and proverbial sayings about contentment (4–6), the advantages of companionship (7–12), and a parable about a poor but wise youth replacing an old foolish king (13–16).

Religious and Cultural Concepts

Vapor as Futility

The Hebrew word translated as “vapor” recurs as a thematic refrain (vv. 4, 7–8, 16), declaring human achievements fleeting. For a more complete discussion, see the Introduction to Ecclesiastes.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Ambiguous Pronoun References

In the parable of the youth and the king (13–16), Hebrew pronouns shift referents without explicit markers. Translators may need to clarify whether “he” refers to the youth or the king.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:6 (#1)
content:
ט֕וֹב מְלֹ֥א כַ֖ף נָ֑חַת מִ⁠מְּלֹ֥א חָפְנַ֛יִם עָמָ֖ל וּ⁠רְע֥וּת רֽוּחַ

"Better {is} a fullness of a palm {with} quiet than a fullness of {two} handfuls {with} toil and pursuit of wind"

Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that contentment with little is better than striving for much. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [One handful with peace is better than two handfuls with toil and chasing after wind]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 4:6 (#2)
content:
מְלֹ֥א כַ֖ף נָ֑חַת

"is} a fullness of a palm {with} quiet"

Qoheleth is speaking as if having a small amount with peace were having a fullness of a palm with quiet. He means that having few possessions and being content is valuable. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a small amount with peace]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 4:6 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠מְּלֹ֥א חָפְנַ֛יִם

"than a fullness of {two} handfuls"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of fullness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [than two hands filled]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:6 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠רְע֥וּת רֽוּחַ

"and pursuit of wind"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 4:7 (#1)
content:
הֶ֖בֶל

"a vapor"

See how you translated this in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#1)
content:
גַּ֣ם בֵּ֧ן וָ⁠אָ֣ח אֵֽין־ל֗⁠וֹ

"even a son or brother, there is not for him"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he does not even have a son or a brother]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#2)
content:
עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ

"his toil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of toil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the hard work he does]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#3)
content:
עיני⁠ו לֹא־תִשְׂבַּ֣ע

"his eye is not satisfied"

Here, his eye represents his desire or appetite. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he is never satisfied]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#4)
content:
עֹ֑שֶׁר

"with} wealth"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wealth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with all that he owns]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠מִ֣י ׀ אֲנִ֣י עָמֵ֗ל וּ⁠מְחַסֵּ֤ר אֶת־נַפְשִׁ⁠י֙ מִ⁠טּוֹבָ֔ה

"So why {am} I toiling and causing my soul to lack from good things"

The lonely person is using the question form to emphasize that there is no good reason for his solitary toil. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So there is no reason for me to toil and cause my soul to lack from good things.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#6)
content:
אֶת־נַפְשִׁ⁠י֙

"my soul"

Here, my soul represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#7)
content:
הֶ֛בֶל

"is} vapor"

See how you translated this in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 4:8 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠עִנְיַ֥ן רָ֖ע הֽוּא

"and it {is} an unpleasant business"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of business, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and it is unpleasant to deal with]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:9 (#1)
content:
שָׂכָ֥ר ט֖וֹב

"a good wage"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wage, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to earn more]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:9 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠עֲמָלָֽ⁠ם

"in exchange for their toil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of toil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in exchange for the work they do]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 4:10 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י אִם־יִפֹּ֔לוּ

"For if they fall"

Qoheleth is presenting a possible condition, that if two companions fall, one can help the other up. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [For if one of them falls]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Ecclesiastes 4:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אִ֣י⁠ל֗⁠וֹ

"but woe {is} his"

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of distress for the person who is alone and falls with no one to help. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [but how terrible it will be for him]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 4:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִֽם־יִתְקְפ⁠וֹ֙ הָ⁠אֶחָ֔ד

"And if he will overpower him, the one {person"

The pronoun he refers to an attacker, while the pronoun him refers to the person who is alone. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And if an attacker overpowers the one person]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 4:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠חוּט֙ הַֽ⁠מְשֻׁלָּ֔שׁ לֹ֥א בִ⁠מְהֵרָ֖ה יִנָּתֵֽק

"and the three-fold rope will not be torn in two quickly"

Qoheleth is speaking as if the bond between three people were a three-fold rope that cannot easily be torn in two. He means that three people united together are very strong. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and three people standing together will not be quickly defeated]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 4:12 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א & יִנָּתֵֽק

"will not be torn in two"

The expression will not be torn in two is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will not break in two]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 4:13 (#1)
content:
ט֛וֹב יֶ֥לֶד מִסְכֵּ֖ן וְ⁠חָכָ֑ם מִ⁠מֶּ֤לֶךְ זָקֵן֙ וּ⁠כְסִ֔יל

"Better {is} a child, poor but wise, than a king, old but foolish"

Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that wisdom is more valuable than power or age. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture.

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 4:13 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠הִזָּהֵ֖ר

"to be warned"

The expression to be warned is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to receive warnings]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 4:14 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠בֵּ֥ית הָ⁠סוּרִ֖ים

"from the house of those who are bound"

Qoheleth is using the house of those who are bound as a common expression of the culture to mean “prison.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from prison]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 4:14 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠סוּרִ֖ים

"those who are bound"

The expression who are bound is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those whom someone had bound]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 4:14 (#3)
content:
יָצָ֣א

"he came forth"

The pronoun he refers to the poor but wise youth from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the poor but wise youth came forth]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 4:14 (#4)
content:
נוֹלַ֥ד רָֽשׁ

"he was born poor"

The expression he was born is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his mother bore him into poverty]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 4:15 (#1)
content:
הַ֣⁠חַיִּ֔ים

"the living"

See how you translated the similar expression in 4:2.

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 4:15 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲמֹ֖ד תַּחְתָּֽי⁠ו

"who will stand under him"

The pronoun him refers to the young king mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [who will stand in his place as the next king]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 4:16 (#1)
content:
אֵֽין־קֵ֣ץ לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֗ם

"There {was} no end to all the people"

Qoheleth says There was no end to all the people as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that there were very many people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [There were very many people]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 4:16 (#2)
content:
לֹ֣א יִשְׂמְחוּ־ב֑⁠וֹ

"will not rejoice in him"

The pronoun him refers to the young king who rose to power. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will not rejoice in that young king]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 4:16 (#3)
content:
הֶ֖בֶל וְ⁠רַעְי֥וֹן רֽוּחַ

"is} vapor and pursuit of wind"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 5 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 5 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from instruction about worship and vows (1–7) to reflection on oppression and wealth (8–17), closing with counsel to enjoy God’s gifts (18–20).

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vows

A person could promise God to do something in return for help. Such a promise was binding, so the writer warns against vowing rashly.

Vapor

The writer calls things “vapor” (7, 10), a recurring image for what is fleeting and empty. See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for a further explanation of this term and its usage.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:1 (#1)
content:
שְׁמֹ֣ר רגלי⁠ך

"Keep your feet"

Qoheleth is using Keep your feet as a common expression of the culture to mean “be careful about how you conduct yourself.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Watch your conduct]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 5:1 (#2)
content:
בֵּ֣ית הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים

"the house of God"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the temple were the house of God, since that was the place where God made his presence known among his people. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple where God dwells]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 5:2 (#1)
content:
עַל־פִּ֜י⁠ךָ

"concerning your mouth"

Here, your mouth represents what you say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [concerning what you say]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לִבְּ⁠ךָ֧ אַל־יְמַהֵ֛ר

"and do not let your heart hurry"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if your thoughts and intentions were your heart. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not let your thoughts hurry you]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 5:2 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֑ים

"to the face of God & the"

Here, to the face of God represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the presence of God]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:2 (#4)
content:
כִּ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֤ים בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ

"For & God {is} in heaven, but you {are} on the earth"

The implication is that God is exalted far above people and so should be addressed with reverence and with few words. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For God is exalted in heaven high above you, and you are lowly here on the earth]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 5:3 (#1)
content:
כִּ֛י בָּ֥א הַ⁠חֲל֖וֹם בְּ⁠רֹ֣ב עִנְיָ֑ן וְ⁠ק֥וֹל כְּסִ֖יל בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב דְּבָרִֽים

"For the dream comes with much business, and the voice of a fool with many words"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [For a fool is certainly known by his excessive talking]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 5:3 (#2)
content:
כִּ֛י בָּ֥א הַ⁠חֲל֖וֹם בְּ⁠רֹ֣ב עִנְיָ֑ן וְ⁠ק֥וֹל כְּסִ֖יל בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב דְּבָרִֽים

"For the dream comes with much business, and the voice of a fool with many words"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific dream or a specific fool. He means dreams and fools in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For some dreams come with much business, and the voice of fools with many words]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 5:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠ק֥וֹל כְּסִ֖יל

"and the voice of a fool"

Here, the voice of a fool represents what a fool says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and what a fool says]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠ק֥וֹל כְּסִ֖יל בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב דְּבָרִֽים

"and the voice of a fool with many words"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the voice of a fool comes with many words]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 5:4 (#1)
content:
תִּדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר

"you vow a vow"

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [you make a vow]

See: Poetry

title: Ecclesiastes 5:4 (#2)
content:
כִּ֛י אֵ֥ין חֵ֖פֶץ בַּ⁠כְּסִילִ֑ים

"for there is no delight in the fools"

The implication is that it is God who has no delight in fools who do not fulfill what they have vowed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for God takes no delight in fools who do not fulfill their vows]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 5:5 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠שֶׁ⁠תִּדּ֖וֹר וְ⁠לֹ֥א תְשַׁלֵּֽם

"than that you vow but do not fulfill"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [than that you make a vow but do not fulfill your vow]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#1)
content:
אַל־תִּתֵּ֤ן אֶת־פִּ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לַ⁠חֲטִ֣יא אֶת־בְּשָׂרֶ֔⁠ךָ

"Do not give your mouth to cause your flesh to sin"

Qoheleth is using Do not give your mouth to cause your flesh to sin as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not let what you say bring guilt upon you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not let what you say bring guilt upon you]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#2)
content:
אֶת־בְּשָׂרֶ֔⁠ךָ

"your flesh"

Qoheleth is using your flesh to represent your whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [yourself]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מַּלְאָ֔ךְ

"the messenger"

The phrase the messenger could mean: (1) the priest who came to collect what a person had vowed to give to God. Alternate translation: [the priest who comes to collect your offering]; or (2) an angel sent by God. Alternate translation: [the angel]. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#4)
content:
כִּ֥י שְׁגָגָ֖ה הִ֑יא

"that it {was} an unintentional sin"

The pronoun it refers to the vow that the person made and did not fulfill. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that your vow was an unintentional sin]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#5)
content:
קוֹלֶ֔⁠ךָ

"your voice"

Here, your voice represents what you have said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your words]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6 (#6)
content:
אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָדֶֽי⁠ךָ

"the deed of your hands"

Here, the deed of your hands represents what you have worked to accomplish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the work you have accomplished]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:7 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י בְ⁠רֹ֤ב חֲלֹמוֹת֙ וַ⁠הֲבָלִ֔ים וּ⁠דְבָרִ֖ים הַרְבֵּ֑ה

"For in many dreams and vaporous things and many words"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For there is futility in many dreams and vaporous things and many words]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 5:7 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠הֲבָלִ֔ים

"and vaporous things"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if things that are empty and fleeting were vaporous things. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and empty, fleeting things]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 5:8 (#1)
content:
עֹ֣שֶׁק רָ֠שׁ וְ⁠גֵ֨זֶל מִשְׁפָּ֤ט וָ⁠צֶ֨דֶק֙

"the} extortion of {the} poor and {the} robbery of justice and equity"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of extortion and robbery, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [poor people being extorted and just and fair treatment being denied]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 5:8 (#2)
content:
מִשְׁפָּ֤ט וָ⁠צֶ֨דֶק֙

"justice and equity"

The phrase justice and equity expresses a single idea. The word equity tells more about justice. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [justice]

See: Hendiadys

title: Ecclesiastes 5:8 (#3)
content:
כִּ֣י גָבֹ֜הַּ מֵ⁠עַ֤ל גָּבֹ֨הַ֙ שֹׁמֵ֔ר

"for a high one over a high one is watching"

The phrase for a high one over a high one is watching could mean: (1) that each official is protected by another official who is more powerful than he is. Alternate translation: [for over each official is a higher official who protects him]; or (2) that God watches over all of them. Alternate translation: [for over each official is a higher official and God watches over all] You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְר֥וֹן אֶ֖רֶץ

"And a profit of a land"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe a profit that is characterized by coming from a land. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the profit that comes from a land]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠כֹּ֣ל היא

"it {is taken} by all"

The expression it is taken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone takes it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (#3)
content:
מֶ֥לֶךְ לְ⁠שָׂדֶ֖ה נֶעֱבָֽד

"But} a king is served by a field"

The expression is served is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But a field provides for a king]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 5:9 (#4)
content:
מֶ֥לֶךְ לְ⁠שָׂדֶ֖ה נֶעֱבָֽד

"But} a king is served by a field"

The implication is that even a king depends on what farmland produces, although it is also possible that Qoheleth means that a king who promotes farming benefits everyone in his land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [But even a king depends on what the fields produce]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 5:10 (#1)
content:
אֹהֵ֥ב כֶּ֨סֶף֙ לֹא־יִשְׂבַּ֣ע כֶּ֔סֶף

"A lover of silver will not be satisfied {with} silver"

Here, silver represents money. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A lover of money will not be satisfied with money]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 5:10 (#2)
content:
אֹהֵ֥ב כֶּ֨סֶף֙

"A lover of silver"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific lover of silver. He means anyone who loves wealth. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone who loves silver]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 5:10 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִֽי־אֹהֵ֥ב בֶּ⁠הָמ֖וֹן לֹ֣א תְבוּאָ֑ה

content:
זֹ֕ה מַתַּ֥ת אֱלֹהִ֖ים הִֽיא

"this, it {is} a gift of God"

title: Ecclesiastes 5:20 (#1)
content:
כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הַרְבֵּ֔ה יִזְכֹּ֖ר אֶת־יְמֵ֣י חַיָּ֑י⁠ו

"with the joys of his heart"

content:

"with the joys of his heart"

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 6 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 6 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Qoheleth continues his examination of wealth and mortality, arguing that neither abundance nor long life benefits a person who is unable to enjoy them.

  1. Wealth that God gives but does not allow a person to enjoy (1–2)
  2. A long, unsatisfied life is worse than a stillborn child (3–6)
  3. Sayings about appetite, wisdom, and desire (7–9)
  4. Human limits before the one who is more powerful (10–12)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 6:7 and 6:9.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vapor

The word rendered “vapor” recurs through this chapter (verses 2, 4, 9, 11, and 12) as the book’s key image for what is fleeting and insubstantial, not for what is morally worthless.

Burial

In this culture a proper burial honored the dead, so the remark that “a burial place is not for him” (3) describes a disgrace rather than merely an absence.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Rhetorical Questions

Qoheleth advances much of his argument by asking questions that expect no answer (verses 6, 8, 11, and 12). If questions do not work this way in your language, you could translate them as statements.

Quoted Sayings

Verses 7 and 9 appear to be popular sayings that Qoheleth quotes in support of his argument. If it would be helpful, you could mark them as quoted sayings.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:1 (#1)
content:
תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"under the sun"

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 (#1)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִתֶּן־ל֣⁠וֹ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֡ים

"A person who the God gives to him"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person. He means anyone in this situation in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone to whom God gives]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 (#2)
content:
עֹשֶׁר֩ וּ⁠נְכָסִ֨ים וְ⁠כָב֜וֹד

"wealth and possessions and honor"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of wealth, possessions, and honor, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [many valuable things that he owns and many people who honor him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠נַפְשׁ֣⁠וֹ ׀ מִ⁠כֹּ֣ל

"for his soul from anything"

Here, his soul represents his appetite. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for his appetite anything]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 (#4)
content:
לֶ⁠אֱכֹ֣ל מִמֶּ֔⁠נּוּ כִּ֛י אִ֥ישׁ נָכְרִ֖י יֹֽאכֲלֶ֑⁠נּוּ

"to eat from it; instead, a nonnative person will eat it"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the wealth that God gives were food that a person could eat. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to enjoy it; instead, a nonnative person will enjoy it]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 (#5)
content:
זֶ֥ה הֶ֛בֶל

"this {is} vapor"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this situation were vapor, which appears for a moment and then is gone. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 9. Alternate translation: [this situation is fleeting and empty]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#1)
content:
אִם־יוֹלִ֣יד אִ֣ישׁ מֵאָ֡ה וְ⁠שָׁנִים֩ רַבּ֨וֹת יִֽחְיֶ֜ה

"If a man should father a hundred {children}, and many years should he live"

Qoheleth is presenting a possible condition, that a man might father many children and live for many years. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Perhaps a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#2)
content:
מֵאָ֡ה

"a hundred {children"

Qoheleth says a hundred children as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [an extremely large number of children]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁנִים֩ רַבּ֨וֹת יִֽחְיֶ֜ה וְ⁠רַ֣ב ׀ שֶׁ⁠יִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵֽי־שָׁנָ֗י⁠ו

"and many years should he live—and many that the days of his years may be"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and he should live an exceedingly great number of years]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠נַפְשׁ⁠וֹ֙ לֹא־תִשְׂבַּ֣ע

"but {if} his soul is not satisfied"

The expression his soul is not satisfied is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but if he does not find satisfaction]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#5)
content:
קְבוּרָ֖ה לֹא־הָ֣יְתָה לּ֑⁠וֹ

"a burial place is not for him"

This could mean: (1) that this man does not receive an honorable burial, which was a great disgrace in this culture. Alternate translation: [he does not even receive an honorable burial]; or (2) that he lives forever and so does not need to be buried. Alternate translation: [if he were to live forever]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 (#6)
content:
אָמַ֕רְתִּי ט֥וֹב מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ הַ⁠נָּֽפֶל

"I say, “Better than him {is} the stillborn child"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [I say that the stillborn child is better than him]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Ecclesiastes 6:4 (#1)
content:
בַ⁠הֶ֥בֶל בָּ֖א וּ⁠בַ⁠חֹ֣שֶׁךְ יֵלֵ֑ךְ

"in vapor, it came, and in the darkness, it will go"

Qoheleth is referring to being born and dying in a polite way by using the phrase in vapor it came, and in the darkness it will go. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [it was conceived, and it died]

See: Euphemism

title: Ecclesiastes 6:4 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בַ⁠חֹ֖שֶׁךְ שְׁמ֥⁠וֹ יְכֻסֶּֽה

"and in the darkness its name will be covered"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the child’s name were an object that the darkness hides from sight. He means that no one ever remembers this child. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and no one will ever remember its name]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 6:4 (#3)
content:
שְׁמ֥⁠וֹ יְכֻסֶּֽה

"its name will be covered"

The expression its name will be covered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one will remember its name]

title: Ecclesiastes 6:5 (#1)
content:
גַּם־שֶׁ֥מֶשׁ לֹא־רָאָ֖ה

"Even {the} sun it did not see"

Qoheleth is using Even the sun it did not see as a common expression of the culture to mean “it never lived.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It never lived]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 6:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָדָ֑ע

"nor did it know"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [nor did it know anything about life]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 6:5 (#3)
content:
נַ֥חַת לָ⁠זֶ֖ה

"More} rest {belongs} to this one"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of rest, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [This one rests better]
