title: Ecclesiastes 6:5 (#4)
content:
לָ⁠זֶ֖ה מִ⁠זֶּֽה

"belongs} to this one than this one"

The pronoun this one occurs twice here. The first instance refers to the stillborn child and the second instance refers to the man who has wealth but does not enjoy it. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [belongs to this stillborn child than to that man]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִלּ֣וּ חָיָ֗ה אֶ֤לֶף שָׁנִים֙ פַּעֲמַ֔יִם

"And if he lived a thousand years twice"

Qoheleth says And if he lived a thousand years twice to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain that even a very long life has no value if a person does not enjoy it. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [And imagine a man who lived a thousand years twice]

See: Hypothetical Situations

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 (#2)
content:
אֶ֤לֶף שָׁנִים֙ פַּעֲמַ֔יִם

"a thousand years twice"

Qoheleth says a thousand years twice as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [an extremely long time]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠טוֹבָ֖ה לֹ֣א רָאָ֑ה

"but a good {thing} he did not see"

Qoheleth is using a good thing he did not see as a common expression of the culture to mean “he did not enjoy his life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he did not enjoy his life]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֛א אֶל־מָק֥וֹם אֶחָ֖ד הַ⁠כֹּ֥ל הוֹלֵֽךְ

"are not both going to one place"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that every person dies, no matter how long he lives. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [both of them certainly go to one place!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 (#5)
content:
אֶל־מָק֥וֹם אֶחָ֖ד הַ⁠כֹּ֥ל הוֹלֵֽךְ

"both going to one place"

Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase going to one place. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [both going to die]

See: Euphemism

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7 (#1)
content:
כָּל־עֲמַ֥ל הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם לְ⁠פִ֑י⁠הוּ וְ⁠גַם־הַ⁠נֶּ֖פֶשׁ לֹ֥א תִמָּלֵֽא

"All the toil of humanity {is} for his mouth, and yet the soul is not filled"

Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to show that people work only to satisfy their appetites and yet are never satisfied. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [All people’s labor goes into their mouths, yet their appetite is never satisfied]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7 (#2)
content:
כָּל־עֲמַ֥ל הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"All the toil of humanity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of toil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [All that humanity works for]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠פִ֑י⁠הוּ

"is} for his mouth"

Here, his mouth represents the food that he eats. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is for the food that he eats]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠נֶּ֖פֶשׁ לֹ֥א תִמָּלֵֽא

"the soul is not filled"

The expression the soul is not filled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing fills the soul]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠נֶּ֖פֶשׁ לֹ֥א תִמָּלֵֽא

"the soul is not filled"

Here, the soul represents the appetite, not the spirit. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the appetite is not satisfied]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 (#1)
content:
כִּ֛י מַה־יּוֹתֵ֥ר לֶ⁠חָכָ֖ם מִֽן־הַ⁠כְּסִ֑יל

"For what advantage {belongs} to the wise more than the fool"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that a wise person has no lasting advantage over a foolish person. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For the wise person has no advantage over the fool!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 (#2)
content:
לֶ⁠חָכָ֖ם מִֽן־הַ⁠כְּסִ֑יל

"belongs} to the wise more than the fool"

Qoheleth is using the adjective the wise as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [belongs to a wise person more than to a foolish person]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 (#3)
content:
מַה־לֶּ⁠עָנִ֣י יוֹדֵ֔עַ לַ⁠הֲלֹ֖ךְ נֶ֥גֶד הַ⁠חַיִּֽים

"What {advantage belongs} to the poor person who knows {how} to walk before the living"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that a poor person who knows how to conduct himself well gains no lasting advantage either. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The poor person who knows how to walk before the living has no advantage either!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠הֲלֹ֖ךְ נֶ֥גֶד הַ⁠חַיִּֽים

"to walk before the living"

Qoheleth is using to walk before the living as a common expression of the culture to mean “to conduct himself well among other people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to conduct himself well among other people]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 (#5)
content:
נֶ֥גֶד הַ⁠חַיִּֽים

"before the living"

Qoheleth is using the adjective the living as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [before people who are alive]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 6:9 (#1)
content:
ט֛וֹב מַרְאֵ֥ה עֵינַ֖יִם מֵֽ⁠הֲלָךְ־נָ֑פֶשׁ

"Better {is} a sight of {the} eyes than the walking of {the} soul"

Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that being content with what a person already has is better than craving what he does not have. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [Better to enjoy what the eyes already see than to crave what one does not have]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 6:9 (#2)
content:
מַרְאֵ֥ה עֵינַ֖יִם

"is} a sight of {the} eyes"

Qoheleth is using a sight of {the} eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “what a person already has.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is what a person already sees before him]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 6:9 (#3)
content:
מֵֽ⁠הֲלָךְ־נָ֑פֶשׁ

"than the walking of {the} soul"

Qoheleth is using the walking of {the} soul as a common expression of the culture to mean “desire that is never satisfied.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [than craving what one does not have]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 6:9 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠רְע֥וּת רֽוּחַ

"and pursuit of wind"

See how you translated pursuit of wind in 1:14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 6:10 (#1)
content:
כְּבָר֙ נִקְרָ֣א שְׁמ֔⁠וֹ

"already its name has been called"

The expression its name has been called is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [already it has a name]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 6:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נוֹדָ֖ע אֲשֶׁר־ה֣וּא אָדָ֑ם

"and it is known what a person {is"

The expression it is known is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people know what a person is]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 6:10 (#3)
content:
ש⁠התקיף מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

"he who is more powerful than him"

The implication is that he who is more powerful than him is God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God, who is far more powerful than any person]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 6:11 (#1)
content:
מַה־יֹּתֵ֖ר לָ⁠אָדָֽם

"what advantage {belongs} to humanity"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that speaking many words brings no benefit to people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [there is no advantage at all for humanity.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י מִֽי־יוֹדֵעַ֩ מַה־טּ֨וֹב לָֽ⁠אָדָ֜ם בַּֽ⁠חַיִּ֗ים מִסְפַּ֛ר יְמֵי־חַיֵּ֥י הֶבְל֖⁠וֹ

"For who is knowing what {is} good for humanity in life {during} the number of the days of his vaporous life"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one knows what is good for a person to do during his brief life. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one knows what is good for humanity in life during the number of the days of his vaporous life.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יַעֲשֵׂ֣⁠ם כַּ⁠צֵּ֑ל

"And he makes them like the shadow"

The point of this comparison is that just as the shadow is brief and quickly gone, so are the days of a person’s life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he makes the days of a person’s life brief and fleeting, quickly gone like a shadow]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יַעֲשֵׂ֣⁠ם

"And he makes them"

The pronoun he refers to God, and the pronoun them refers to the days of a person’s life. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And God makes the days of a person’s life]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁר֙ מִֽי־יַגִּ֣יד לָֽ⁠אָדָ֔ם מַה־יִּהְיֶ֥ה אַחֲרָ֖י⁠ו תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"For who will declare to humanity what will be after him under the sun"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to tell a person what will happen after he dies. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one will declare to humanity what will be after him under the sun.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 (#5)
content:
מַה־יִּהְיֶ֥ה אַחֲרָ֖י⁠ו

"what will be after him"

Here, what will be after him could mean: (1) what will happen after he dies. Alternate translation: [what will happen after he dies]; or (2) what will happen to him later in life. Alternate translation: [what will happen to him in the future]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 7 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter first gathers proverbs about wisdom, mortality, and the limits of human understanding, and then records Qoheleth’s own search for understanding.

  1. Better-than proverbs about mourning, grief, and rebuke (1–6)
  2. Further proverbs about patience, anger, and the protection wisdom gives (7–12)
  3. A call to consider God’s work in good times and bad (13–14)
  4. Counsel about righteousness, wisdom, and human sinfulness (15–22)
  5. Qoheleth’s search for the scheme of things (23–29)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 7:1–12, 14–18, and 26–29.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Better-than sayings

Many verses in this chapter use a proverb form that sets two things side by side and declares one of them more advantageous than the other. The comparison is practical rather than absolute: it commends what teaches a person about life, not what feels pleasant.

Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears again in this chapter in verses 6 and 15. Render it consistently through the book.

Fearing God

In verse 18, the person who fears God is the person who reverently acknowledges God’s rule and lives accordingly. This is respectful submission, not terror.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

The heart

Throughout the chapter, “heart” stands for the inner person: thoughts, inclination, and moral judgment. If your readers would not understand this use of “heart,” consider a term in your language that refers to the seat of thinking and deciding.

The woman in verse 26

Interpreters understand the woman in verse 26 in two ways: (1) a specific kind of seductive woman who entraps men or (2) folly pictured as a woman. The ULT preserves the figure so that either reading remains possible.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (#1)
content:
ט֥וֹב שֵׁ֖ם מִ⁠שֶּׁ֣מֶן ט֑וֹב

"Better is a {good} name than good oil"

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that what people remember about a person is worth more than what money can buy. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [A good name is better than fine perfume]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (#2)
content:
שֵׁ֖ם

"a {good} name"

Here, name represents a person’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a good reputation]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠שֶּׁ֣מֶן ט֑וֹב

"than good oil"

The implication is that good oil is expensive perfumed oil, which people in this culture valued highly. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [than costly perfumed oil]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠י֣וֹם הַ⁠מָּ֔וֶת מִ⁠יּ֖וֹם הִוָּלְדֽ⁠וֹ

"and the day of death than the day of his being born"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and better is the day of death than the day of his being born]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠יּ֖וֹם הִוָּלְדֽ⁠וֹ

"than the day of his being born"

The expression his being born is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [than the day when his mother bore him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 7:2 (#1)
content:
בֵּֽית־אֵ֗בֶל מִ⁠לֶּ֨כֶת֙ אֶל־בֵּ֣ית מִשְׁתֶּ֔ה

"a house of mourning than to go to a house of a banquet"

Here, a house of mourning and a house of a banquet represent the gatherings that people hold in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a funeral than to go to a feast]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 7:2 (#2)
content:
ה֖וּא ס֣וֹף כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָ֑ם

"it {is} the end of all humanity"

Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase the end of all humanity. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [death is what awaits all humanity]

See: Euphemism

title: Ecclesiastes 7:2 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠חַ֖י יִתֵּ֥ן אֶל־לִבּֽ⁠וֹ

"and the living will give {it} to his heart"

Qoheleth is using will give {it} to his heart as a common expression of the culture to mean “will think carefully about it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the living should reflect seriously on that]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:2 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠חַ֖י

"and the living"

Qoheleth is using the adjective the living as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and a person who is alive]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 7:3 (#1)
content:
ט֥וֹב כַּ֖עַס מִ⁠שְּׂחֹ֑ק

"Better grief than laughter"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of grief and laughter, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Better to grieve than to laugh]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 7:3 (#2)
content:
בְ⁠רֹ֥עַ פָּנִ֖ים

"with a bad face"

Qoheleth is using a bad face as a common expression of the culture to mean “a sad expression.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with a sad expression]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:3 (#3)
content:
יִ֥יטַב לֵֽב

"a heart may be well"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s inner self were his heart. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person may be well within himself]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:4 (#1)
content:
לֵ֤ב חֲכָמִים֙ בְּ⁠בֵ֣ית אֵ֔בֶל

"The} heart of wise people {is} in a house of mourning"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the thoughts and inclinations of wise people were their heart, which could be in a place. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Wise people set their minds on a house of mourning]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:5 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠אִ֕ישׁ שֹׁמֵ֖עַ שִׁ֥יר כְּסִילִֽים

"than a person listening to a song of fools"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [than for someone to listen to a song of fools]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 7:5 (#2)
content:
שִׁ֥יר כְּסִילִֽים

"a song of fools"

The implication is that a song of fools is entertainment and flattery that pleases a person but teaches him nothing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the pleasant but empty singing of fools]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:6 (#1)
content:
כְ⁠ק֤וֹל הַ⁠סִּירִים֙ תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠סִּ֔יר כֵּ֖ן שְׂחֹ֣ק הַ⁠כְּסִ֑יל

"like the sound of the thorns under the cooking pot, so {is} the laughter of the fool"

The point of this comparison is that just as the sound of the thorns under the cooking pot is loud but produces almost no heat, so is the laughter of the fool loud but worth nothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as thorns crackle loudly under the cooking pot but give almost no heat, so the laughter of the fool is loud but accomplishes nothing]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 7:6 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠סִּירִים֙ תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠סִּ֔יר

"the thorns under the cooking pot"

Qoheleth is using words with similar sounds for poetic effect. In the original language, the word for the thorns sounds almost the same as the word for the cooking pot. You may want to reproduce this effect if poetry in your language does this.

See: Poetry

title: Ecclesiastes 7:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠גַם־זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל

"And this also {is} vapor"

See how you translated the similar expression in 6:2. Alternate translation: [And this also is like a passing breath]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:7 (#1)
content:
כִּ֥י הָ⁠עֹ֖שֶׁק יְהוֹלֵ֣ל חָכָ֑ם וִֽ⁠יאַבֵּ֥ד אֶת־לֵ֖ב מַתָּנָֽה

"Surely oppression crazes {a} wise {person}, and a bribe destroys a heart"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Surely corrupt gain completely ruins the mind of even a wise person]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 7:7 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠עֹ֖שֶׁק יְהוֹלֵ֣ל חָכָ֑ם

"oppression crazes {a} wise {person"

Qoheleth is speaking of oppression as if it were a living thing that could drive a person out of his mind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a wise person loses his mind when others oppress him]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 7:7 (#3)
content:
וִֽ⁠יאַבֵּ֥ד אֶת־לֵ֖ב מַתָּנָֽה

"and a bribe destroys a heart"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s ability to judge rightly were his heart. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a bribe destroys a person’s ability to judge rightly]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:8 (#1)
content:
אֶֽרֶךְ־ר֖וּחַ

"is} length of spirit"

Qoheleth is using length of spirit as a common expression of the culture to mean “patience.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is patience]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:8 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠גְּבַהּ־רֽוּחַ

"than height of spirit"

Qoheleth is using height of spirit as a common expression of the culture to mean “pride.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [than pride]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:9 (#1)
content:
אַל־תְּבַהֵ֥ל בְּ⁠רֽוּחֲ⁠ךָ֖ לִ⁠כְע֑וֹס

"Do not hasten in your spirit to become angry"

Qoheleth is using hasten in your spirit to become angry as a common expression of the culture to mean “become angry quickly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not become angry quickly]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:9 (#2)
content:
כַ֔עַס בְּ⁠חֵ֥יק כְּסִילִ֖ים יָנֽוּחַ

"anger rests in {the} lap of fools"

Qoheleth is speaking of anger as if it were a living thing that could settle down and rest in a person’s lap. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fools are characterized by anger]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 7:10 (#1)
content:
מֶ֣ה הָיָ֔ה שֶׁ֤⁠הַ⁠יָּמִים֙ הָ⁠רִ֣אשֹׁנִ֔ים הָי֥וּ טוֹבִ֖ים מֵ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה

"What was, that the former days were better than these"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [What was the reason that the former days were better than these days]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 7:11 (#1)
content:
טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה עִֽם־נַחֲלָ֑ה

"Wisdom is good with an inheritance"

The implication is that Wisdom brings the kind of benefit that wealth brings. This could mean that wisdom is: (1) as good as an inheritance or (2) good along with an inheritance. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Wisdom is as valuable as an inheritance]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:11 (#2)
content:
טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה עִֽם־נַחֲלָ֑ה

"Wisdom is good with an inheritance"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of Wisdom and an inheritance, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [To be wise is good along with what a person inherits]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 7:11 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠רֹאֵ֥י הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"to those who see the sun"

Qoheleth is using those who see the sun as a common expression of the culture to mean “people who are alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who are living]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠צֵ֥ל הַֽ⁠חָכְמָ֖ה בְּ⁠צֵ֣ל הַ⁠כָּ֑סֶף

"as} in the shadow of wisdom, {so} in the shadow of silver"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the protection that wisdom and money give a person were the shadow that they cast. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as wisdom gives protection, so also does silver give protection]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠כָּ֑סֶף

"silver"

Here, silver represents money and possessions in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [riches]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְר֣וֹן דַּ֔עַת

"And {this is} an advantage of knowledge"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe an advantage that knowledge gives a person. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And this is an advantage that knowledge gives a person]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 7:12 (#4)
content:
הַֽ⁠חָכְמָ֖ה תְּחַיֶּ֥ה בְעָלֶֽי⁠הָ

"Wisdom preserves her owners"

Qoheleth is speaking of Wisdom as if it were a living thing that could keep alive the people who have it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Being wise keeps people alive]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 7:13 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠תַקֵּ֔ן אֵ֖ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִוְּתֽ⁠וֹ

"to straighten that which he has bent"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the way that God orders events were something that God had bent and no one could straighten. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to change what he has determined]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:14 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠י֤וֹם טוֹבָה֙ הֱיֵ֣ה בְ⁠ט֔וֹב וּ⁠בְ⁠י֥וֹם רָעָ֖ה רְאֵ֑ה

"In a day of good, be in good, but in a day of misfortune, see"

Qoheleth is referring to all of the circumstances of a person’s life by naming two extremes, a day of good and a day of misfortune. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In whatever circumstances you find yourself, consider this]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 7:14 (#2)
content:
הֱיֵ֣ה בְ⁠ט֔וֹב

"be in good"

Qoheleth is using be in good as a common expression of the culture to mean “enjoy what is good.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [enjoy the good things]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:14 (#3)
content:
אֶת־זֶ֤ה לְ⁠עֻמַּת־זֶה֙ עָשָׂ֣ה הָֽ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים

"the God has done this as well as this"

The first occurrence of the pronoun this refers to a day of good, while the second refers to a day of misfortune. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God has made the day of good as well as the day of misfortune]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:14 (#4)
content:
שֶׁ⁠לֹּ֨א יִמְצָ֧א הָֽ⁠אָדָ֛ם אַחֲרָ֖י⁠ו מְאֽוּמָה

"humanity cannot find anything after him"

Qoheleth is using cannot find anything after him as a common expression of the culture to mean “cannot discover what God has planned.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [humanity cannot discover what God has planned]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:15 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠ימֵ֣י הֶבְלִ֑⁠י

"in the days of my vapor"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if his lifetime were vapor, which appears for a moment and then is gone. See how you translated the similar expression in 1:14. Alternate translation: [in the days of my brief life]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:15 (#2)
content:
אֹבֵ֣ד בְּ⁠צִדְק֔⁠וֹ

"perishing in his righteousness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of his righteousness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [perishing even though he acts righteously]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 7:15 (#3)
content:
מַאֲרִ֖יךְ בְּ⁠רָעָתֽ⁠וֹ

"lengthening in his evil"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lengthening his days in his evil]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 7:16 (#1)
content:
אַל־תְּהִ֤י צַדִּיק֙ הַרְבֵּ֔ה

"Do not be overly righteous"

The implication is that Qoheleth is warning against a kind of excess, not against being righteous. This could mean: (1) being self-righteous. Alternate translation: [Do not be self-righteous]; or (2) being excessively scrupulous about doing what is right. Alternate translation: [Do not be excessively scrupulous]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:16 (#2)
content:
לָ֖⁠מָּה תִּשּׁוֹמֵֽם

"why should you be shocked"

The expression be shocked is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [why should life shock you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 7:17 (#1)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה תָמ֖וּת בְּ⁠לֹ֥א עִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ

"why should you die when {it is} not your time"

Qoheleth is using the question form to warn his readers about the consequence of being wicked and foolish. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [otherwise you will die before your time has come!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 7:17 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠לֹ֥א עִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ

"when {it is} not your time"

Qoheleth is using not your time as a common expression of the culture to mean “before the time when you would otherwise die.” This could mean: (1) that the person dies needlessly young because of their own foolishness. Alternate translation: [sooner than you need to]; or (2) that God cuts their life short. Alternate translation: [because God is displeased with your wickedness]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:18 (#1)
content:
תֶּאֱחֹ֣ז בָּ⁠זֶ֔ה וְ⁠גַם־מִ⁠זֶּ֖ה

"you should take hold of this, and also from this"

The first occurrence of the pronoun this refers to the warning against being overly righteous and wise, while the second refers to the warning against being wicked and foolish. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you should take hold of this warning against being overly righteous and wise, and also from that warning against being wicked and foolish]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:18 (#2)
content:
תֶּאֱחֹ֣ז בָּ⁠זֶ֔ה

"you should take hold of this"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if his advice were an object that a person could take hold of. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you should pay attention to this advice]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:18 (#3)
content:
אַל־תַּנַּ֣ח אֶת־יָדֶ֑⁠ךָ

"do not let your hand rest"

Qoheleth is using do not let your hand rest as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not let go of it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not loosen your grip]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:18 (#4)
content:
יֵצֵ֥א אֶת־כֻּלָּֽ⁠ם

"will go forth with both of them"

Qoheleth is using will go forth with both of them as a common expression of the culture to mean “will come safely through both of these.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will come safely through both of these dangers]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:19 (#1)
content:
הַֽ⁠חָכְמָ֖ה תָּעֹ֣ז לֶ⁠חָכָ֑ם מֵֽ⁠עֲשָׂרָה֙ שַׁלִּיטִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָי֖וּ בָּ⁠עִֽיר

"Wisdom is strong for the wise, more than ten rulers who are in the city"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if wisdom were a defense that makes a person strong, the way that rulers defend a city. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Wisdom protects the wise person better than ten rulers can protect the city]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:19 (#2)
content:
לֶ⁠חָכָ֑ם

"for the wise"

Qoheleth is using the adjective the wise as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for a wise person]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 7:19 (#3)
content:
מֵֽ⁠עֲשָׂרָה֙ שַׁלִּיטִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָי֖וּ בָּ⁠עִֽיר

"more than ten rulers who are in the city"

Qoheleth says ten rulers as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means a large number of powerful officials. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [more than a whole group of powerful rulers in the city]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 7:20 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י אָדָ֔ם אֵ֥ין צַדִּ֖יק בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"For a person—there is not a righteous {person} on the earth"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about a person with the information about there not being a righteous {person} on the earth. Alternate translation: [For there is not a righteous person among the people on the earth]

See: Information Structure

title: Ecclesiastes 7:20 (#2)
content:
אֵ֥ין צַדִּ֖יק בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲשֶׂה־טּ֖וֹב וְ⁠לֹ֥א יֶחֱטָֽא

"there is not a righteous {person} on the earth who does good and does not sin"

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to state that every person sins. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [no righteous man walks the earth who does only good and never sins]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 7:21 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠כָל־הַ⁠דְּבָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְדַבֵּ֔רוּ אַל־תִּתֵּ֖ן לִבֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"to all of the words that they say, do not give your heart"

If it would be helpful in your language, you could change the order of these phrases. Alternate translation: [do not give your heart to all of the words that they say]

See: Information Structure

title: Ecclesiastes 7:21 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְדַבֵּ֔רוּ

"that they say"

Qoheleth is using the pronoun they in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that anyone says]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:21 (#3)
content:
אַל־תִּתֵּ֖ן לִבֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"do not give your heart"

Qoheleth is using do not give your heart as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not pay attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not listen to them]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:21 (#4)
content:
אֶֽת־עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֖ מְקַלְלֶֽ⁠ךָ

"your servant belittling you"

The implication is that it would be especially painful to hear your servant speak badly of you, since a servant owed his master respect. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [even your own servant, who owes you respect, speaking badly of you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:22 (#1)
content:
יָדַ֣ע לִבֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"your heart knows"

Qoheleth is using your heart knows as a common expression of the culture to mean “you yourself are aware.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you know]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:22 (#2)
content:
גַּם־את קִלַּ֥לְתָּ אֲחֵרִֽים

"even you have belittled others"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as have belittled already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that his readers have done the very thing that they would not want to hear. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [even you yourself have belittled others]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:22 (#3)
content:
אֲחֵרִֽים

"others"

Qoheleth is using the adjective others as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [other people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes 7:23 (#1)
content:
בַֽ⁠חָכְמָ֑ה

"with wisdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wisdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by thinking wisely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 7:23 (#2)
content:
אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֶחְכָּ֔מָה

"I said, “Let me be wise"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that I would be wise,]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Ecclesiastes 7:23 (#3)
content:
רְחוֹקָ֥ה מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

"was} far from me"

Qoheleth is using far from me as a common expression of the culture to mean “beyond my ability to understand.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was beyond what I could understand]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 7:24 (#1)
content:
רָח֖וֹק מַה־שֶּׁ⁠הָיָ֑ה וְ⁠עָמֹ֥ק ׀ עָמֹ֖ק

"Far away {is} that which was. And deep, deep"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if what he wanted to understand were Far away and deep in a place that he could not reach. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Beyond understanding is that which was. And profoundly mysterious]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:24 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָמֹ֥ק ׀ עָמֹ֖ק

"And deep, deep"

Qoheleth is repeating forms of the word deep in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And extremely deep]

See: Reduplication

title: Ecclesiastes 7:24 (#3)
content:
מִ֥י יִמְצָאֶֽ⁠נּוּ

"who can find it"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to understand these things. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one can find it.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 7:25 (#1)
content:
סַבּ֨וֹתִֽי אֲנִ֤י וְ⁠לִבִּ⁠י֙

"I turned, I, and my heart"

Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a living thing that could search alongside him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I turned with all my mind]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 7:25 (#2)
content:
סַבּ֨וֹתִֽי אֲנִ֤י וְ⁠לִבִּ⁠י֙

"I turned, I, and my heart"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I turned already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself gave his whole attention to this search. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself turned my whole heart]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:25 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠דַ֣עַת וְ⁠לָ⁠ת֔וּר וּ⁠בַקֵּ֥שׁ

"to know and to explore and {to} seek"

The terms to know, to explore, and {to} seek mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to diligently search out]

See: Doublet

title: Ecclesiastes 7:25 (#4)
content:
רֶ֣שַׁע כֶּ֔סֶל וְ⁠הַ⁠סִּכְל֖וּת הוֹלֵלֽוֹת

"the} wickedness {that is} folly and the foolishness {that is} madness"

The terms {the} wickedness {that is} folly and the foolishness {that is} madness mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [how completely senseless wicked madness is]

See: Doublet

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#1)
content:
מַ֣ר מִ⁠מָּ֗וֶת

"more bitter than death"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the distress that this woman causes were a taste that was more bitter than death. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [more painful to endure than dying]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הָֽ⁠אִשָּׁה֙ אֲשֶׁר־הִ֨יא מְצוֹדִ֧ים

"the woman who, she {is} snares"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun she separately, even though the phrase the woman who already indicates whom he is talking about. He is doing that to emphasize what this woman is like. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [the woman who is truly nothing but snares]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#3)
content:
אֶת־הָֽ⁠אִשָּׁה֙ אֲשֶׁר־הִ֨יא

"the woman who, she {is"

The implication is that Qoheleth is describing something that traps a man and ruins him. This could mean: (1) a seductive woman. Alternate translation: [the seductive woman, and she is]; or (2) folly, which Qoheleth pictures as a woman. Alternate translation: [the folly, and it is] You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠חֲרָמִ֛ים לִבָּ֖⁠הּ אֲסוּרִ֣ים יָדֶ֑י⁠הָ

"and nets, her heart; chains, her hands"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and her heart is a net, and her hands are chains]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠חֲרָמִ֛ים לִבָּ֖⁠הּ

"and nets, her heart"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this woman’s intentions were nets for catching a man. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and her heart, intent on catching men]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#6)
content:
אֲסוּרִ֣ים יָדֶ֑י⁠הָ

"chains, her hands"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this woman’s hold on a man were chains. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [her hands hold a man tightly so that he cannot escape]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#7)
content:
ט֞וֹב לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י

"One who is} good to the face of"

See how you translated the similar expression in 2:26.

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠חוֹטֵ֖א יִלָּ֥כֶד בָּֽ⁠הּ

"but a sinner will be captured by her"

The expression will be captured is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but she will capture a sinner]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 7:27 (#1)
content:
רְאֵה֙ זֶ֣ה מָצָ֔אתִי אָמְרָ֖ה קֹהֶ֑לֶת

"See, this I have found,” says Qoheleth"

The phrase says Qoheleth introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Ecclesiastes 7:27 (#2)
content:
אַחַ֥ת לְ⁠אַחַ֖ת לִ⁠מְצֹ֥א חֶשְׁבּֽוֹן

"One to one to find the scheme of things"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I examined one thing after another in order to find the scheme of things]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 7:27 (#3)
content:
קֹהֶ֑לֶת

"Qoheleth"

See how you translated this name in 1:1.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Ecclesiastes 7:28 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֛ר עוֹד־בִּקְשָׁ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֖⁠י וְ⁠לֹ֣א מָצָ֑אתִי

"while still my soul sought, but I have not found"

title: Ecclesiastes 7:28 (#2)
content:
בִּקְשָׁ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֖⁠י

"my soul sought"

Here, my soul represents the seeker himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I kept searching]

title: Ecclesiastes 7:28 (#3)
content:
אָדָ֞ם אֶחָ֤ד מֵ⁠אֶ֨לֶף֙ מָצָ֔אתִי וְ⁠אִשָּׁ֥ה בְ⁠כָל־אֵ֖לֶּה לֹ֥א מָצָֽאתִי

"One man from a thousand {men} I found, but a woman among all of these {people}, I did not find"

title: Ecclesiastes 7:28 (#4)
content:
אָדָ֞ם אֶחָ֤ד מֵ⁠אֶ֨לֶף֙

"One man from a thousand {men"

Qoheleth says a thousand {men} as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means a very large number of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [One man from a very great number of men]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 7:29 (#1)
content:
עָשָׂ֧ה הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם יָשָׁ֑ר

"the God made humanity upright"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if living rightly were standing upright. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God made people to live rightly]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 7:29 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֵ֥מָּה בִקְשׁ֖וּ חִשְּׁבֹנ֥וֹת רַבִּֽים

"but they, they have sought out many schemes"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun they along with the verb translated as have sought out, which already includes its meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting what God did with what humanity has done. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [but they have sought out many schemes]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 7:29 (#3)
content:
חִשְּׁבֹנ֥וֹת רַבִּֽים

"many schemes"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of schemes, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they might scheme in many ways]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 8 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 8 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from wise conduct before a king to the injustice that Qoheleth observes, and it ends by affirming that no one can fully understand what God does.

  1. The value of wisdom (1)
  2. Wise conduct before a king (2–9)
    1. Obeying the king’s command (2–4)
    2. Knowing the right time and the limits of human power (5–9)
  3. The wicked seem to escape judgment (10–14)
  4. Commendation of joy (15)
  5. The limits of understanding God’s work (16–17)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 8:1, 8:5–8, and 8:11–14.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The oath of God

In verse 2, Qoheleth grounds obedience to the king in an oath connected with God. This likely refers to a promise of loyalty to the king that people made in God’s name, though it could refer to God’s own oath concerning the king.

Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears again in this chapter in verses 10 and 14. Render it consistently through the book.

Fearing God

In verses 12 and 13, those who fear God are people who reverently acknowledge his rule and live accordingly. This is respectful submission, not terror.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Generic “him”

In several verses (6, 7, 15, and 17), “him” and “he” refer to people in general rather than to a specific person. If your language would not use a singular pronoun this way, you could use a plural or general expression.

Textual variant in verse 10

Most Hebrew manuscripts say that the wicked were “forgotten” in the city, while some manuscripts and ancient versions say that they were “praised.” The ULT follows the second reading.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1 (#1)
content:
מִ֚י כְּ⁠הֶ֣⁠חָכָ֔ם וּ⁠מִ֥י יוֹדֵ֖עַ פֵּ֣שֶׁר דָּבָ֑ר

"Who {is} like the wise person, and who knows {the} interpretation of a matter"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is like the wise person, because only a wise person knows the interpretation of a matter. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [No one is like the wise person, and no one else knows the interpretation of a matter!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1 (#2)
content:
פֵּ֣שֶׁר דָּבָ֑ר

"the} interpretation of a matter"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of interpretation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what a matter means]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1 (#3)
content:
חָכְמַ֤ת אָדָם֙

"The} wisdom of a person"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wisdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [That a person is wise]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1 (#4)
content:
תָּאִ֣יר פָּנָ֔י⁠ו

"enlightens his face"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if wisdom were a light that enlightens a person’s face. He means that wisdom gives a person a cheerful or gracious expression. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [gives him a cheerful expression]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠עֹ֥ז פָּנָ֖י⁠ו יְשֻׁנֶּֽא

"and the strength of his face is changed"

Qoheleth is using the strength of his face as a common expression of the culture to mean “his harsh or stern expression.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his harsh expression is changed] or [and it changes his harsh expression]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:2 (#1)
content:
פִּי־מֶ֣לֶךְ

"the mouth of a king"

Here, mouth represents the king’s commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the commands of a king]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 8:2 (#2)
content:
שְׁבוּעַ֥ת אֱלֹהִֽים

"the oath of God"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe an oath that involves God. This could mean: (1) an oath of loyalty to the king that a person made in the presence of God or (2) an oath that God made to support the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the oath that you swore before God]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 8:3 (#1)
content:
תִּבָּהֵ֤ל מִ⁠פָּנָי⁠ו֙

"Do & be terrified from his face"

Here, face represents the presence of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verse 12. Alternate translation: [Do not let fear of this king control you]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 8:3 (#2)
content:
אַֽל־תַּעֲמֹ֖ד בְּ⁠דָבָ֣ר רָ֑ע

"Do not stand in a bad matter"

Qoheleth is using Do not stand in a bad matter as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not join in or continue with an evil plan.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not take part in an evil plan]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:4 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֥י יֹֽאמַר־ל֖⁠וֹ מַֽה־תַּעֲשֶֽׂה

"And who will say to him, “What are you doing"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [And who will ask him what he is doing]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Ecclesiastes 8:4 (#2)
content:
מַֽה־תַּעֲשֶֽׂה

"What are you doing"

Qoheleth is imagining someone using the question form to challenge or rebuke the king for what he is doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not do what you are doing!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 8:5 (#1)
content:
לֹ֥א יֵדַ֖ע דָּבָ֣ר רָ֑ע

"will not know a bad matter"

Qoheleth is using will not know a bad matter as a common expression of the culture to mean “will not experience harm.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not experience any harm]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:5 (#2)
content:
לֵ֥ב חָכָֽם

"the} heart of a wise {person"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart of a wise person were the part of him that thinks and understands. He means the mind of a wise person. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the mind of a wise person]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 8:6 (#1)
content:
כִּֽי־רָעַ֥ת הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם רַבָּ֥ה עָלָֽי⁠ו

"because the misfortune of humanity {is} severe upon him"

Qoheleth uses the word because here to indicate a contrast between the fact that there is a proper time and procedure for every matter and the fact that people suffer great misfortune. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [even though the misfortune of humanity is severe upon him]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Ecclesiastes 8:6 (#2)
content:
רָעַ֥ת הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"the misfortune of humanity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of misfortune, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what troubles humanity]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 8:6 (#3)
content:
עָלָֽי⁠ו

"upon him"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person by him. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [upon people]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 8:7 (#1)
content:
מִ֖י יַגִּ֥יד לֽ⁠וֹ

"who will declare {it} to him"

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one can tell a person what will happen in the future. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one can declare it to him.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 8:8 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־יְמַלֵּ֥ט רֶ֖שַׁע אֶת־בְּעָלָֽי⁠ו

"and wickedness will not deliver its masters"

Qoheleth is speaking of wickedness as if it were a living thing that could deliver its masters. He means that doing wicked things will not save wicked people from death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and wicked people will not escape death by doing wicked things]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 8:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָת֣וֹן אֶת־לִבִּ֔⁠י

"while} giving my heart"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:13. This also occurs in verse 16.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:9 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠כָֽל־מַעֲשֶׂ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נַעֲשָׂ֖ה

"to every deed that was done"

The expression was done is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to every deed that people did]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 8:9 (#3)
content:
תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"under the sun"

See how you translated under the sun in 1:3. This also occurs in verses 15 and 17.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:9 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠רַ֥ע לֽ⁠וֹ

"to his harm"

The pronoun his refers to a person who suffers harm. This could mean: (1) the person over whom someone else has authority. Alternate translation: [to the harm of the person he rules over]; or (2) the person who has authority, who brings harm on himself by harming others. Alternate translation: [to his own harm, he brings harm to another] It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#1)
content:
רְשָׁעִ֨ים קְבֻרִ֜ים

"wicked people buried"

The expression buried is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people burying the bodies of wicked people]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠בָ֗אוּ וּ⁠מִ⁠מְּק֤וֹם קָדוֹשׁ֙ יְהַלֵּ֔כוּ

"and they entered, and from a place of holiness they went"

The implication is that while these wicked people were alive, they regularly went into and out of a place of holiness, that is, the temple. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and while they were alive, they regularly entered and left the holy place, the temple]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יִֽשְׁתַּכְּח֥וּ

"And they were praised"

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “And they were forgotten.” Other ancient manuscripts read “And they were praised.” The ULT follows that reading. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר כֵּן־עָשׂ֑וּ

"where thus they had done"

The implication is that these wicked people had done evil deeds in the same city where people praised them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [where they had done these evil deeds]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#5)
content:
גַּם־זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל

"This also {is} vapor"

The pronoun This refers to something that Qoheleth says is vapor. This could mean: (1) the situations that Qoheleth describes in the next two verses. Alternate translation: [What I am about to describe also is vapor]; or (2) the situation that he has just described in this verse. Alternate translation: [People praising the wicked actions of others is also vapor] It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. This also occurs in verse 14.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10 (#6)
content:
גַּם־זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל

"This also {is} vapor"

See how you translated this same word in 1:2. This word also occurs in verse 14.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 8:11 (#1)
content:
אֵין־נַעֲשָׂ֣ה פִתְגָ֔ם מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה הָ⁠רָעָ֖ה מְהֵרָ֑ה

"a decree {against} the evil deed is not made quickly"

The expression is not made is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those in authority do not quickly make a decree against the evil deed]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 8:11 (#2)
content:
מָלֵ֞א לֵ֧ב בְּֽנֵי־הָ⁠אָדָ֛ם בָּ⁠הֶ֖ם לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת רָֽע

"the heart of the sons of humanity fills in them to do evil"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart of people were a container that fills with the desire to do evil. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people become fully determined to do evil]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 8:11 (#3)
content:
בְּֽנֵי־הָ⁠אָדָ֛ם

"the sons of humanity"

See how you translated the sons of humanity in 1:13.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:12 (#1)
content:
מְאַ֖ת

"a hundred times"

Qoheleth says a hundred times as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means very many times. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [over and over again]

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 8:12 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מַאֲרִ֣יךְ ל֑⁠וֹ

"and lengthening {days} for himself"

Qoheleth is using lengthening days for himself as a common expression of the culture to mean “living a long life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and living a long life]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:13 (#1)
content:
יַאֲרִ֥יךְ יָמִ֖ים כַּ⁠צֵּ֑ל

"will he lengthen {his} days like & shadow"

The point of this comparison is that just as the shadow soon passes away, so the life of a wicked person will come to an end. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [will he lengthen his days, which pass away quickly like a shadow]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 8:14 (#1)
content:
הֶבֶל֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֣ה עַל־הָ⁠אָרֶץ֒

"vapor that is done on the earth"

The expression is done is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [vapor that happens on the earth]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 8:14 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה הָ⁠רְשָׁעִ֔ים & כְּ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה הַ⁠צַּדִּיקִ֑ים

"like the deeds of the wicked people & like the deeds of the righteous people"

The implication is that righteous people experience what wicked people deserve for their deeds, and wicked people experience what righteous people deserve for their deeds. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to what the wicked people deserve for their deeds … according to what the righteous people deserve for their deeds]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 8:14 (#3)
content:
זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל

"this {is} vapor"

See how you translated the similar expression in 6:2.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 8:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שִׁבַּ֤חְתִּֽי אֲנִי֙

"And I praised, I"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as praised already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this is his own conclusion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And I myself praised]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 8:15 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠שִּׂמְחָ֔ה

"joy"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of joy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people being joyful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 8:15 (#3)
content:
אֵֽין־ט֤וֹב לָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שֶּׁ֔מֶשׁ כִּ֛י אִם־לֶ⁠אֱכ֥וֹל וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁתּ֖וֹת וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׂמ֑וֹחַ

"there is nothing good for humanity under the sun except to eat and to drink and to rejoice"

If it would appear in your language that Qoheleth was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [the only good thing for humanity under the sun is to eat and to drink and to rejoice]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Ecclesiastes 8:15 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠ה֞וּא יִלְוֶ֣⁠נּוּ בַ⁠עֲמָל֗⁠וֹ

"And it will accompany him in his toil"

Qoheleth is speaking of joy as if it were a living thing that could accompany him in his toil. He means that a person can experience joy while he works hard. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will be able to experience joy in his toil]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 8:16 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הָ֣⁠עִנְיָ֔ן אֲשֶׁ֥ר נַעֲשָׂ֖ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"the business that is done on the earth"

The expression is done is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the business that people do on the earth]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 8:16 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּוֹם֙ וּ⁠בַ⁠לַּ֔יְלָה

"in the day and in the night"

Qoheleth is referring to all of the time by naming two major components, the day and the night. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at all times]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 8:16 (#3)
content:
שֵׁנָ֕ה בְּ⁠עֵינָ֖י⁠ו אֵינֶ֥⁠נּוּ רֹאֶֽה

"sleep in his eyes he is not seeing"

Qoheleth is using sleep in his eyes he is not seeing as a common expression of the culture to mean “he does not sleep at all.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is not sleeping at all]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 8:16 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠עֵינָ֖י⁠ו אֵינֶ֥⁠נּוּ רֹאֶֽה

"in his eyes he is not seeing"

The pronouns his and he refer to someone who does not sleep. This could mean: (1) any person who is busy with the business that is done on the earth. Alternate translation: [in his eyes a person who is busy with that business is not seeing]; or (2) Qoheleth himself, who is speaking of himself in the third person. Alternate translation: [in my eyes, who am busy with that business, am not seeing]. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 8:17 (#1)
content:
לֹ֨א יוּכַ֜ל הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם לִ⁠מְצוֹא֙ אֶת־הַֽ⁠מַּעֲשֶׂה֙

"humanity is not able to find the deed"

Qoheleth is using find as a common expression of the culture to mean “understand.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 9 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 9 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter reflects on death as the one event that comes to every person, urges readers to enjoy life while they can, and ends with a story showing that wisdom is valuable even when people do not honor it.

  1. The same fate comes to everyone (1–3)
  2. The living have hope, but the dead are forgotten (4–6)
  3. A call to enjoy life and work with all your strength (7–10)
  4. Time and misfortune overtake all people (11–12)
  5. The value of wisdom (13–18)
    1. The poor wise man who delivered a city (13–15)
    2. Sayings about wisdom (16–18)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 9:2, 9:4–6, 9:11–12, and 9:17–18.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Sheol

In verse 10, Hades is the place of the dead, where Qoheleth says there is no more work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom. Use a term that refers to the place where people go when they die, not a place of punishment.

White clothes and oil

In verse 8, wearing white clothes and putting oil on the head were signs of joy and celebration in the culture of that time. If your readers would not understand these as signs of joy, you could explain them in a footnote.

Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears twice in verse 9. Render it consistently through the book.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“One happening”

In verses 2 and 3, the “one happening” that comes to everyone is death. Translate this in a way that makes clear that Qoheleth is speaking about the fate that all people share, whether they are righteous or wicked.
