title: Ecclesiastes 9:12 (#5)
content:
כְּ⁠שֶׁ⁠תִּפּ֥וֹל עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם פִּתְאֹֽם

"when it falls upon them suddenly"

Qoheleth is using when it falls upon them suddenly as a common expression of the culture to mean “when misfortune happens to them unexpectedly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when it happens to them unexpectedly]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 9:13 (#1)
content:
זֹ֛ה רָאִ֥יתִי חָכְמָ֖ה תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"this I saw: Wisdom under the sun"

The pronoun this refers to the example of Wisdom that Qoheleth describes in the next two verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I saw the following example of wisdom under the sun]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 9:13 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠גְדוֹלָ֥ה הִ֖יא אֵלָֽ⁠י

"and great it {was} to me"

Qoheleth is using great it was to me as a common expression of the culture to mean “it impressed me greatly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it impressed me greatly]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 9:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֥ים & מְעָ֑ט

"and a few men"

Here the masculine term men has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and a few people]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Ecclesiastes 9:15 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מָ֣צָא בָ֗⁠הּ

"And he found in it"

The pronoun he refers to someone who found the poor wise man. This could mean: (1) the king from the previous verse found this man in the city. Alternate translation: [And the king found in it]; or (2) an unspecified person found this man in the city. Alternate translation: [And there was found in it]. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 9:15 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִלַּט־ה֥וּא אֶת־הָ⁠עִ֖יר בְּ⁠חָכְמָת֑⁠וֹ

"and he himself delivered the city with his wisdom"

The implication is that the wisdom of the poor wise man was able to save the city from the king. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he himself delivered the city from the king by giving wise advice]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 9:15 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠חָכְמָת֑⁠וֹ

"with his wisdom"

See how you translated the similar expression in 8:1.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 9:15 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אָדָם֙ לֹ֣א זָכַ֔ר

"But a person did not remember"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person. He means people in general, so that no one remembered that poor man. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But no one remembered]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַ֣רְתִּי אָ֔נִי טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה מִ⁠גְּבוּרָ֑ה וְ⁠חָכְמַ֤ת הַ⁠מִּסְכֵּן֙ בְּזוּיָ֔ה וּ⁠דְבָרָ֖י⁠ו אֵינָ֥⁠ם נִשְׁמָעִֽים

"And I said, I, “Better {is} wisdom than might, but the wisdom of the poor person {is} despised, and his words—they are not heard"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [And I said that wisdom is better than might, but the wisdom of the poor person is despised, and his words are not heard]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַ֣רְתִּי אָ֔נִי

"And I said, I"

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as said already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this is his own conclusion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And I myself said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (#3)
content:
טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה מִ⁠גְּבוּרָ֑ה

"Better {is} wisdom than might"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of wisdom and might, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Better is it to be wise than to be strong]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠חָכְמַ֤ת הַ⁠מִּסְכֵּן֙ בְּזוּיָ֔ה

"but the wisdom of the poor person {is} despised"

The expression {is} despised is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but people despise the wisdom of the poor person]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠דְבָרָ֖י⁠ו אֵינָ֥⁠ם נִשְׁמָעִֽים

"and his words—they are not heard"

The expression they are not heard is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people do not listen to his words]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17 (#1)
content:
דִּבְרֵ֣י חֲכָמִ֔ים בְּ⁠נַ֖חַת נִשְׁמָעִ֑ים מִ⁠זַּעֲקַ֥ת מוֹשֵׁ֖ל בַּ⁠כְּסִילִֽים

"The} words of wise people in quietness are heeded more than the cry of a ruler among the fools"

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to show that the quiet words of wise people are more valuable than the shouting of a ruler who leads foolish people. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [People listen more to the quiet words of the wise than to the shouting of a ruler over fools]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17 (#2)
content:
דִּבְרֵ֣י חֲכָמִ֔ים בְּ⁠נַ֖חַת נִשְׁמָעִ֑ים

"The} words of wise people in quietness are heeded"

The expression are heeded is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People heed the words of wise people in quietness]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠נַ֖חַת

"in quietness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of quietness, you could express the same idea in another way. This could mean: (1) that wise people who speak their words quietly are heeded. Alternate translation: [spoken quietly]; or (2) that people listen calmly to the words of a wise person. Alternate translation: [calmly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠זַּעֲקַ֥ת מוֹשֵׁ֖ל בַּ⁠כְּסִילִֽים

"more than the cry of a ruler among the fools"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [more than the cry of a ruler among the fools is heeded]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠כְּסִילִֽים

"among the fools"

Qoheleth is using the adjective translated as fools as a noun to mean people who are foolish. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [among foolish people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 10 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 10 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a collection of short wisdom sayings that contrast the wise person with the foolish person, especially in how each one acts, works, and speaks, and in how rulers govern.

  1. A little folly ruins much wisdom (1–3)
  2. Rulers and those under them (4–7)
    1. Stay calm when a ruler is angry (4)
    2. Rulers who give high positions to the wrong people (5–7)
  3. Wisdom and the dangers of ordinary work (8–11)
  4. The words of the wise and the words of fools (12–15)
  5. Sayings about rulers, work, and speech (16–20)
    1. Foolish rulers and noble rulers (16–17)
    2. Laziness, feasting, and money (18–19)
    3. Do not curse the king even in private (20)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 10:1–20.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Right and left

In verse 2, the right side was associated with strength, protection, and favor and the left side with weakness and misfortune. If your readers would not understand this association, you could express the meaning plainly or explain it in a footnote.

Snake charming

In verse 11, the “master of the tongue” is a snake charmer, a person who used words or sounds to calm snakes so they would not bite. His skill is useless if the snake bites before he uses it.

Feasting in the morning

In verse 16, princes who “eat in the morning” are feasting when they should be working, which showed that they did not take their responsibilities seriously.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Proverbs

Most verses in this chapter are proverbs that are only loosely connected to one another. Translate them in a way that sounds like a wise saying in your language and keep each one short and memorable.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:1 (#1)
content:
זְב֣וּבֵי מָ֔וֶת

"Flies of death"

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe Flies that are characterized by death. This could mean: (1) flies that have died. Alternate translation: [Dead flies]; or (2) flies that bring death or disease. Alternate translation: [Flies that bring death] If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way.

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 10:1 (#2)
content:
יָקָ֛ר מֵ⁠חָכְמָ֥ה מִ⁠כָּב֖וֹד סִכְל֥וּת מְעָֽט

"weightier than wisdom or honor {is} a little foolishness"

The point of this comparison is that just as Flies of death can spoil a whole container of a perfumer’s oil, so a little foolishness can spoil the good that wisdom and honor have accomplished. Qoheleth implies this comparison by placing the two statements next to each other. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the same way, a little foolishness can spoil the good that wisdom or honor has accomplished]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 10:2 (#1)
content:
לֵ֤ב & וְ⁠לֵ֥ב

"The} heart of & but a heart of"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s mind and will were his heart. It means that what a person thinks and desires guides the way he lives. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The mind of … but the mind of]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:2 (#2)
content:
חָכָם֙ & כְּסִ֖יל

"a wise person & a fool"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific wise person or a specific fool. He means wise people and foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whoever is wise … whoever is foolish]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 10:2 (#3)
content:
לִֽ⁠ימִינ֔⁠וֹ & לִ⁠שְׂמֹאלֽ⁠וֹ

"to his right & to his left"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart could turn to his right or to his left. In this culture, the right side represented strength and favor, and the left side represented weakness or misfortune. This could mean: (1) a wise person’s understanding protects him, while a fool is exposed to harm. Alternate translation: [it can protect him … it leaves him defenseless]; or (2) a wise person is inclined toward what is good, while a fool is inclined toward what is evil. Alternate translation: [it leads him toward what is good … it leads him toward what is evil]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:3 (#1)
content:
לִבּ֣⁠וֹ חָסֵ֑ר

"his heart {is} lacking"

Qoheleth is using the expression that his heart is lacking as a common expression of the culture to mean “he lacks good sense.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his mind lacks good sense]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַ֥ר לַ⁠כֹּ֖ל

"and it says to everyone {that} he"

Qoheleth is speaking of the fool’s lack of sense as if it were a living thing that could speak to everyone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his behavior shows everyone that he]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 10:4 (#1)
content:
ר֤וּחַ הַ⁠מּוֹשֵׁל֙ תַּעֲלֶ֣ה עָלֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"the spirit of the ruler rises against you"

Qoheleth is using the spirit of the ruler rises against you as a common expression of the culture to mean “the ruler becomes angry with you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ruler becomes angry with you]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:4 (#2)
content:
מְקוֹמְ⁠ךָ֖ אַל־תַּנַּ֑ח

"do not leave your place"

Qoheleth is using do not leave your place as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not abandon your position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not resign from your post]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:4 (#3)
content:
מַרְפֵּ֔א

"calmness"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of calmness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [remaining calm]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:4 (#4)
content:
יַנִּ֖יחַ חֲטָאִ֥ים גְּדוֹלִֽים

"will cause great sins to leave"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if great sins were things that could be caused to leave. This could mean: (1) staying calm will cause the ruler to overlook great offenses. Alternate translation: [can reduce the king’s anger at the offenses]; or (2) staying calm will keep you from committing great sins, such as rebelling against the ruler. Alternate translation: [can keep great offenses from having their effect]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:5 (#1)
content:
תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"under the sun"

See how you translated under the sun in 1:3.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:5 (#2)
content:
כִּ⁠שְׁגָגָ֕ה

"like an unintentional sin"

The point of this comparison is that just as an unintentional sin that a ruler commits causes harm even though he did not intend it, so is the misfortune that Qoheleth saw harmful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [which was harmful like an unintentional sin]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 10:5 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠שַּׁלִּֽיט

"from before the face of the authority"

Here, the face represents the presence of the authority. The expression means that the error comes from the ruler himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the authority himself]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 10:6 (#1)
content:
נִתַּ֣ן הַ⁠סֶּ֔כֶל

"Folly is placed"

The expression Folly is placed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is the ruler mentioned in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [The ruler places folly] or [The ruler places foolish people]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 10:6 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠סֶּ֔כֶל

"Folly"

Here, Folly represents foolish people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The foolish person]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 10:6 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠מְּרוֹמִ֖ים רַבִּ֑ים וַ⁠עֲשִׁירִ֖ים בַּ⁠שֵּׁ֥פֶל יֵשֵֽׁבוּ

"into many high places, and rich {people} sit in the lowly place"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if important positions were high places and unimportant positions were the lowly place. It means that foolish people are given positions of honor and authority, while rich people are given positions of little importance. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into many positions of honor, and rich people sit in positions of little importance]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:7 (#1)
content:
רָאִ֥יתִי עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־סוּסִ֑ים וְ⁠שָׂרִ֛ים הֹלְכִ֥ים כַּ⁠עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"Indeed, I saw slaves on horses and princes walking like slaves on the ground"

Verses 6 and 7 mean basically the same thing. Verse 6 states the general idea, and verse 7 gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [Indeed, I saw the social order reversed, with slaves holding high positions and princes brought low]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 10:7 (#2)
content:
עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־סוּסִ֑ים

"slaves on horses"

The implication is that only important and wealthy people rode horses, while slaves walked. Qoheleth is saying that the normal order of society has been reversed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [slaves riding on horses as if they were important and wealthy people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:8 (#1)
content:
חֹפֵ֥ר גּוּמָּ֖ץ בּ֣⁠וֹ יִפּ֑וֹל וּ⁠פֹרֵ֥ץ גָּדֵ֖ר יִשְּׁכֶ֥⁠נּוּ נָחָֽשׁ

"One who digs a pit will fall into it, and one who breaks through a wall—a snake will bite him"

Here Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to warn that people who do risky actions often suffer the consequences of those actions. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [Whoever digs a hole may fall into it, and whoever tears down a wall may be bitten by a snake]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 10:8 (#2)
content:
יִשְּׁכֶ֥⁠נּוּ נָחָֽשׁ

"a snake will bite him"

The implication is that snakes often lived in the cracks of stone walls, so a person who breaks through a wall could be bitten by a snake hiding in it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a snake hiding in the cracks of that wall will bite him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:9 (#1)
content:
מַסִּ֣יעַ אֲבָנִ֔ים יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בּוֹקֵ֥עַ עֵצִ֖ים יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽ⁠ם

"Indeed, one who pulls up stones will be hurt by them; one who splits wood will be endangered by them"

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that every kind of work carries its own risks, so a wise person takes care while doing it. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. This verse emphasizes the meaning of verse 8 by repeating the same idea using different words. Alternate translation: [Whoever moves stones may be injured by them; whoever chops logs may be harmed by them]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 10:9 (#2)
content:
מַסִּ֣יעַ אֲבָנִ֔ים יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בּוֹקֵ֥עַ עֵצִ֖ים יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽ⁠ם

"Indeed, one who pulls up stones will be hurt by them; one who splits wood will be endangered by them"

Verses 8 and 9 mean basically the same thing. Verse 9 emphasizes the meaning of verse 8 by repeating the same idea using different words. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [Indeed, one who pulls up stones or splits wood will be hurt by them]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 10:9 (#3)
content:
יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם

"will be hurt by them"

The expression will be hurt is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The word them refers to the stones. Alternate translation: [will find that they hurt him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 10:9 (#4)
content:
יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽ⁠ם

"will be endangered by them"

The expression will be endangered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The word them refers to the split pieces of wood. Alternate translation: [will find that the pieces endanger him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 10:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הוּא֙ לֹא־פָנִ֣ים קִלְקַ֔ל

"but he himself does not lighten the faces"

Qoheleth is using lighten the faces as a common expression of the culture to mean “sharpen the cutting edge.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. The pronoun he refers to the person who is using the axe to cut wood. Alternate translation: [but the person using the axe does not sharpen its cutting edge]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְר֥וֹן הכשיר חָכְמָֽה

"But a profit to succeeding {is} wisdom"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of profit, succeeding, and wisdom, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [But if a person acts wisely, it will help him to succeed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:11 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠לוֹא־לָ֑חַשׁ

"without a charm"

The implication is that the snake bites someone before the snake charmer has used a charm to calm it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [before the snake charmer has used a charm to calm it]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:11 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בַ֖עַל הַ⁠לָּשֽׁוֹן

"for the master of the tongue"

Qoheleth is using the master of the tongue as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who charms snakes with his words.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the snake charmer]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:12 (#1)
content:
דִּבְרֵ֥י פִי־חָכָ֖ם חֵ֑ן וְ⁠שִׂפְת֥וֹת כְּסִ֖יל תְּבַלְּעֶֽ⁠נּוּ

"The} words of {the} mouth of a wise {person are} favor, but {the} lips of a fool will swallow him"

Here Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that wise people speak in ways that bring them goodwill, while fools destroy themselves by what they say. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [What a wise person says brings him goodwill, but what a fool says will destroy him]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 10:12 (#2)
content:
חֵ֑ן

"are} favor"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of favor, you could express the same idea in another way. This could mean: (1) the words of a wise person are gracious and pleasing. Alternate translation: [are gracious and pleasing]; or (2) the words of a wise person win him the goodwill of others. Alternate translation: [brings him goodwill]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:13 (#1)
content:
תְּחִלַּ֥ת דִּבְרֵי־פִ֖י⁠הוּ סִכְל֑וּת וְ⁠אַחֲרִ֣ית פִּ֔י⁠הוּ הוֹלֵל֖וּת רָעָֽה

"The beginning of the words of his mouth {is} foolishness, and {the} end of his mouth {is} evil insanity"

Qoheleth is referring to the whole of a fool’s speech by naming two extremes, The beginning of the words of his mouth and the end of his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [At first the words of his mouth are foolishness, and in the end what he says is evil insanity]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 10:13 (#2)
content:
הוֹלֵל֖וּת רָעָֽה

"is} evil insanity"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of insanity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is wickedly insane]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:14 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אָדָם֙

"Humanity"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person when he says Humanity and him. He means people in general, not the fool mentioned earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A person]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 10:14 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר יִֽהְיֶה֙ מֵֽ⁠אַחֲרָ֔י⁠ו

"and that which will be after him"

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and does not know what will happen after he is gone]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 10:14 (#3)
content:
מִ֖י יַגִּ֥יד

"who will declare {it"

Qoheleth is using the question form for emphasis. He means that no one can tell a person what will happen after him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one at all can declare it]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Ecclesiastes 10:15 (#1)
content:
תְּיַגְּעֶ֑⁠נּוּ

"wearies him"

The pronoun him refers to each one of the foolish people mentioned earlier in the verse. Qoheleth changes from the plural to the singular here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [wearies each one of them]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 10:15 (#2)
content:
לֹֽא־יָדַ֖ע לָ⁠לֶ֥כֶת אֶל־עִֽיר

"he does not know {how} to go to a city"

Qoheleth is using the expression he does not know how to go to a city as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is so foolish that he cannot even find his way to town.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is too foolish to find even the most obvious path]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 10:16 (#1)
content:
אִֽי־לָ֣⁠ךְ

"Woe to you"

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief about the trouble that will come to a land with such leaders. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for you]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 10:16 (#2)
content:
אֶ֔רֶץ

"land"

Qoheleth is speaking to a land that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the harm that bad rulers cause to a nation. He is using land to mean the people who live in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the land. Alternate translation: [people of the land]

See: Apostrophe

title: Ecclesiastes 10:16 (#3)
content:
נָ֑עַר

"is} a youth"

The implication is that a king who is a youth is not able to rule well. This could mean: (1) the king is young and inexperienced. Alternate translation: [is too young and inexperienced to rule well]; or (2) the king is a person of low birth, such as a servant, since the word translated youth can also mean “servant.” Alternate translation: [is not able to rule well]. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:16 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠שָׂרַ֖יִ⁠ךְ בַּ⁠בֹּ֥קֶר יֹאכֵֽלוּ

"and your princes eat in the morning"

The implication is that your princes are feasting in the morning, when they should be working to govern the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and your princes feast in the morning when they should be governing you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:17 (#1)
content:
אַשְׁרֵ֣י⁠ךְ אֶ֔רֶץ שֶׁ⁠מַּלְכֵּ֖⁠ךְ בֶּן־חוֹרִ֑ים וְ⁠שָׂרַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ בָּ⁠עֵ֣ת יֹאכֵ֔לוּ בִּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א בַ⁠שְּׁתִֽי

"Blessed are you, land, that your king {is} a son of nobles and {that} your princes will eat at the time with might and not with drunkenness"

Verses 16 and 17 mean basically the same thing. For emphasis, Qoheleth is saying it first negatively and then positively. If a speaker of your language would not use repetition like this, in your translation you can convey the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Blessed are you, land, that your king is a son of nobles and that your princes will eat at the proper time only to gain strength]

See: Parallelism

title: Ecclesiastes 10:17 (#2)
content:
אַשְׁרֵ֣י⁠ךְ

"Blessed are you"

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of happiness for a land that has good leaders. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy you are]

See: Exclamations

title: Ecclesiastes 10:17 (#3)
content:
בֶּן־חוֹרִ֑ים

"is} a son of nobles"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a descendant of noble people were their son. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is from a noble family]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:17 (#4)
content:
בָּ⁠עֵ֣ת

"at the time"

The implication is that the princes eat and drink only at the proper time for meals, not early in the morning as described in the previous verse. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the proper time for meals]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 10:17 (#5)
content:
בִּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א בַ⁠שְּׁתִֽי

"with might and not with drunkenness"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of might and drunkenness, you could express the same ideas in another way. This could mean that the princes eat: (1) to gain strength, rather than to get drunk. Alternate translation: [to become strong and not to get drunk]; or (2) with self-control, rather than in a drunken way. Alternate translation: [with moderation and not over-indulgence]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:18 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠עֲצַלְתַּ֖יִם יִמַּ֣ךְ הַ⁠מְּקָרֶ֑ה וּ⁠בְ⁠שִׁפְל֥וּת יָדַ֖יִם יִדְלֹ֥ף הַ⁠בָּֽיִת

"With laziness, the beams of the roof sink, and in idleness of hands, the house will leak"

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that neglecting needed work leads to damage and loss. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [When people are lazy, the roof timbers give way, and when people’s hands do nothing, the house lets in rain]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 10:18 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠עֲצַלְתַּ֖יִם

"With laziness"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of laziness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When people are lazy]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 10:18 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠שִׁפְל֥וּת יָדַ֖יִם

"and in idleness of hands"

Qoheleth is using hands to represent the people who should be working with them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and when people are idle]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 10:19 (#1)
content:
לֶ֔חֶם

"bread"

Qoheleth is using bread to represent food in general, especially the food served at a feast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a feast]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 10:19 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠כֶּ֖סֶף

"but silver"

Here, silver represents money. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but money]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 10:19 (#3)
content:
יַעֲנֶ֥ה אֶת־הַ⁠כֹּֽל

"answers everything"

Qoheleth is speaking of silver as if it were a living thing that could answer people. He means that money can provide everything that people need. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is useful for obtaining everything]

See: Personification

title: Ecclesiastes 10:20 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠מַדָּֽעֲ⁠ךָ֗

"in your thought"

The pronoun your refers to anyone who reads Qoheleth’s words. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in your thought, my reader]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 10:20 (#2)
content:
ע֤וֹף הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ יוֹלִ֣יךְ אֶת־הַ⁠קּ֔וֹל

"a bird of the heavens will carry the voice"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a bird of the heavens could carry the voice of a person to others. It means that what you say in private may be reported to the people you speak about in ways you would not expect. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you say may be reported as if a bird of the heavens had carried it]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 10:20 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בַ֥עַל ה⁠כנפים

"and a master of wings"

Qoheleth is using a master of wings as a common expression of the culture to mean “a bird.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a winged creature]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 11 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 11 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter urges readers to act diligently and generously even though they cannot know what the future holds, and then to enjoy life, especially in youth, while remembering that God will judge them.

  1. Acting wisely despite an uncertain future (1–6)
    1. Give generously, since no one knows what misfortune may come (1–2)
    2. Do not wait for perfect conditions before working (3–4)
    3. No one knows what God is doing, so keep working (5–6)
  2. Enjoy life while remembering the days of darkness (7–8)
  3. Counsel to the young man: enjoy your youth, but know that God will judge you (9–10)

The counsel to the young man in verses 9–10 continues into 12:1–8, so translators may want to keep the end of this chapter connected with the beginning of the next.

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 11:1–4 and 11:6–8.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears again in this chapter in verses 8 and 10. Render it consistently through the book.

God’s judgment

In verse 9, Qoheleth tells the young man to enjoy life but to know that God will judge him for all that he does. The call to enjoy life is therefore not permission to live carelessly.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

What people cannot know

The phrase “you do not know” or “you are not knowing” recurs in verses 2, 5, and 6, and it ties the chapter’s advice together: because people cannot know the future or the work of God, they should act wisely and diligently now. If possible, translate these phrases in a similar way so that readers can see the connection.

Proverbs with uncertain meaning

The sayings in verses 1–2 are brief and figurative, and scholars understand them in different ways, such as being generous to others or spreading out one’s trade or investments. Translate them in a way that allows for these meanings if possible. (See: Proverbs)

title: Ecclesiastes 11:1 (#1)
content:
שַׁלַּ֥ח לַחְמְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠מָּ֑יִם כִּֽי־בְ⁠רֹ֥ב הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים תִּמְצָאֶֽ⁠נּוּ

"Throw your bread on the face of the waters, for in many days you will find it"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s goods or efforts were bread thrown on the face of the waters, by which he means that they are given away in some sense. This could refer to: (1) being generous to others, which will bring a reward later, as in the UST, or (2) being willing to risk making an investment in something that should bring a profit at a future time. Alternate translation: [make investments now, because they will bring profit to you later]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:2 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠שִׁבְעָ֖ה וְ⁠גַ֣ם לִ⁠שְׁמוֹנָ֑ה

"to seven and even to eight"

Qoheleth is using to seven and even to eight as a common expression of the culture to mean “to many.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to many people]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 11:2 (#2)
content:
כִּ֚י לֹ֣א תֵדַ֔ע מַה־יִּהְיֶ֥ה רָעָ֖ה עַל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"for you do not know what will be a misfortune on the earth"

The implication is that these seven or eight people will help you when you are in need because you helped them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for you do not know what will be a misfortune on the earth, and when it happens, they will help you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 11:3 (#1)
content:
יִמָּלְא֨וּ הֶ⁠עָבִ֥ים גֶּ֨שֶׁם֙

"the clouds are filled with rain"

The expression are filled is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the clouds are full of rain]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 11:3 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠דָּר֖וֹם וְ⁠אִ֣ם בַּ⁠צָּפ֑וֹן

"in the south or in the north"

Qoheleth is referring to all of the places where a tree might fall by naming two major components, the south and the north. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in one direction or another]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 11:4 (#1)
content:
שֹׁמֵ֥ר ר֖וּחַ לֹ֣א יִזְרָ֑ע וְ⁠רֹאֶ֥ה בֶ⁠עָבִ֖ים לֹ֥א יִקְצֽוֹר

"One who attends {to the} wind will not sow, and one who watches {the} clouds will not harvest"

Here Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that people who wait for perfect conditions will never accomplish anything. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [One who keeps waiting for a perfect wind will never sow, and one who keeps waiting for perfect skies will never harvest]

See: Proverbs

title: Ecclesiastes 11:5 (#1)
content:
דֶּ֣רֶךְ הָ⁠ר֔וּחַ

"is} the way of the wind"

The implication is that the way of the wind is something that people cannot understand. This could mean: (1) how the wind moves, where it comes from, and where it goes. Alternate translation: [is the path of the wind, where it comes from and where it goes]; or (2) how the breath of life enters the body of an unborn child, since the word translated wind can also mean “spirit” or “breath.” Alternate translation: [is the breath of life, where it comes from and how it gives life]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 11:5 (#2)
content:
כַּ⁠עֲצָמִ֖ים

"as the bones"

Qoheleth is using the bones to represent the whole body of the unborn baby. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the parts of the baby’s body]

See: Synecdoche

title: Ecclesiastes 11:5 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מְּלֵאָ֑ה

"the full {woman"

Qoheleth is using the full woman as a common expression of the culture to mean “the pregnant woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the woman who is pregnant]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 11:6 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ זְרַ֣ע אֶת־זַרְעֶ֔⁠ךָ וְ⁠לָ⁠עֶ֖רֶב

"In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening"

Qoheleth is referring to all of the day by naming two major components, In the morning and in the evening. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [From morning until evening sow your seed, and]

See: Merism

title: Ecclesiastes 11:6 (#2)
content:
אַל־תַּנַּ֣ח יָדֶ֑⁠ךָ

"do not let your hand rest"

Here, hand represents the person working with their hands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [do not stop working]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 11:6 (#3)
content:
הֲ⁠זֶ֣ה אוֹ־זֶ֔ה

"this one or this one"

The first this one refers to the seed sown in the morning, while the second this one refers to the seed sown in the evening. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the morning seed or the evening seed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 11:7 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מָת֖וֹק הָ⁠א֑וֹר

"And light {is} sweet"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if light, which represents being alive, were something that tastes sweet. It means that being alive is pleasant. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And being alive is pleasant]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:7 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠ט֥וֹב לַֽ⁠עֵינַ֖יִם לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת אֶת־הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"and {it is} good for the eyes to see the sun"

Qoheleth is using it is good for the eyes to see the sun as a common expression of the culture to mean “it is good to be alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it is good to be living]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 11:8 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"the man"

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific man. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a person]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 11:8 (#2)
content:
יִשְׂמָ֑ח וְ⁠יִזְכֹּר֙

"let him rejoice, but let him remember"

Qoheleth is saying what he wants any person who lives many years to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that he rejoice, but he should remember]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Ecclesiastes 11:8 (#3)
content:
אֶת־יְמֵ֣י הַ⁠חֹ֔שֶׁךְ

"the days of darkness"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a time of death or trouble were darkness. This could mean: (1) the time after a person dies, when he will no longer see the light of the sun. Alternate translation: [the days when he will be dead]; or (2) times of trouble and sorrow during a person’s life. Alternate translation: [the days of trouble in his life]. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly.

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:8 (#4)
content:
כָּל־שֶׁ⁠בָּ֥א הָֽבֶל

"Everything that is coming {is} vapor"

See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for more information on this term. See how you translated this in 1:2 Alternate translation: [Everything that is coming is temporary and quickly passes away]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:9 (#1)
content:
בָּח֣וּר

"young man"

Here the masculine term young man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [young person]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Ecclesiastes 11:9 (#2)
content:
וִֽ⁠יטִֽיבְ⁠ךָ֤ לִבְּ⁠ךָ֙

"and let your heart make you glad"

Qoheleth is saying what he wants the young man’s heart to do. Alternate translation: [and I want your heart to make you glad]

See: Third-Person Imperatives

title: Ecclesiastes 11:9 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַלֵּךְ֙ בְּ⁠דַרְכֵ֣י לִבְּ⁠ךָ֔ וּ⁠בְ⁠מַרְאֵ֖י עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"And walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the way a person lives were walking on a path. He speaks of doing what a person desires as walking in the ways of your heart and of doing what a person sees and likes as walking in the sight of your eyes. It means that the young man should live by doing what he wants and what he sees that he likes. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And live by doing what you desire and what you see that you like]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:9 (#4)
content:
יְבִֽיאֲ⁠ךָ֥ & בַּ⁠מִּשְׁפָּֽט

"will bring you into judgment"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of judgment, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will bring you before him and judge you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 11:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָסֵ֥ר כַּ֨עַס֙ מִ⁠לִּבֶּ֔⁠ךָ וְ⁠הַעֲבֵ֥ר רָעָ֖ה מִ⁠בְּשָׂרֶ֑⁠ךָ

"And remove anger from your heart and take misfortune away from your flesh"

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if anger and misfortune were objects that a person could take away from his heart and his flesh. It means that the young man should not let himself stay angry or let troubles affect him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And do not stay angry, and do not let troubles affect your body]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 11:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַֽ⁠שַּׁחֲר֖וּת

"and dark hair"

Here, dark hair represents “the prime of life.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the prime of life]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes - Chapter 12 Introduction
content:
Ecclesiastes 12 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes Qoheleth’s counsel to the young person from 11:9–10, repeats the book’s opening refrain, and then closes the book with words about Qoheleth and a final command to fear God.

  1. Remember your Creator before old age and death come (1–7)
    1. Before the days of misfortune come (1–2)
    2. Pictures of the weakness of old age (3–5)
    3. Pictures of death (6–7)
  2. The final refrain: everything is vapor (8)
  3. Words about Qoheleth and the sayings of the wise (9–12)
    1. Qoheleth’s work as a teacher (9–10)
    2. The value and limits of wise sayings (11–12)
  4. The conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments (13–14)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 12:1–7 and 12:13–14.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Vapor

The refrain in verse 8 repeats the words of 1:2, so that the book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial frames everything Qoheleth has said. Render it the same way you did in chapter 1.

Death as a return

In verse 7, the body that God formed from dust returns to the earth, and the spirit that God gave returns to him. Verse 5 similarly calls the grave a person’s “eternal home.”

Fearing God and God’s judgment

The book ends by telling people to fear God and keep his commandments, because God will bring every deed into judgment. This is reverent submission to God, not terror.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Pictures of old age

Verses 2–6 describe old age and death through a long series of images, such as a house whose guards tremble, grinders that stop working, and a lamp and a well that break. Many interpreters understand these as pictures of a weakening body, while others take them as a literal household and town in decline. If possible, keep the images so that readers can see this extended picture.

Qoheleth spoken about in the third person

From verse 8 to the end of the book, someone speaks about Qoheleth instead of Qoheleth speaking for himself. Make sure that it is clear in your translation that a different speaker is now describing Qoheleth and his teaching.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:1 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠זְכֹר֙ אֶת־בּ֣וֹרְאֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"So, remember your Creator"

Qoheleth is using remember as a common expression of the culture to mean “keep in mind and honor.” He is not talking about recalling something that a person has forgotten. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So, honor your Creator and keep him in mind]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 12:1 (#2)
content:
עַ֣ד אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹא־יָבֹ֨אוּ֙ יְמֵ֣י הָֽ⁠רָעָ֔ה וְ⁠הִגִּ֣יעוּ שָׁנִ֔ים

"when the days of misfortune have not come and the years arrive"

Qoheleth is using the phrase when the days of misfortune have not come to mean “before the days of misfortune come.” The negation also applies to the years arrive, so the meaning is “before the years arrive.” Your language may have a connecting word or phrase that you can use to show that the young person should remember his Creator before this time comes. Alternate translation: [before the days of misfortune come and before the years arrive]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Ecclesiastes 12:1 (#3)
content:
יְמֵ֣י הָֽ⁠רָעָ֔ה

"the days of misfortune"

The implication is that the days of misfortune are the time of old age, when a person experiences weakness, pain, and other troubles. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the days of old age when you will have weakness and pain]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 12:1 (#4)
content:
תֹּאמַ֔ר

"you will say"

The term you will say introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Ecclesiastes 12:2 (#1)
content:
לֹֽא־תֶחְשַׁ֤ךְ הַ⁠שֶּׁ֨מֶשׁ֙ וְ⁠הָ⁠א֔וֹר וְ⁠הַ⁠יָּרֵ֖חַ וְ⁠הַ⁠כּוֹכָבִ֑ים

"the sun and the light and the moon and the stars have not darkened"

Qoheleth is speaking as if what happens to a person in old age were the sun, the moon, and the stars becoming darkened. This could mean: (1) that the joy and strength of a person’s life fades in old age, just as the lights in the sky grow dark. Alternate translation: [your joy and strength have not faded like the light of the sun, the moon, and the stars growing dark]; or (2) that an old person’s eyesight grows dim, so that even the lights in the sky seem dark. Alternate translation: [your eyes have not grown so dim that the sun, the moon, and the stars seem dark to you]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁ֥בוּ הֶ⁠עָבִ֖ים אַחַ֥ר הַ⁠גָּֽשֶׁם

"and the clouds return after the rain"

Qoheleth is speaking as if the troubles of old age were the clouds that return after the rain. He means that in old age one trouble follows another without relief, just as storm clouds come back again even after it has already rained. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and one trouble keeps coming after another without relief]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:3 (#1)
content:
שֶׁ⁠יָּזֻ֨עוּ֙ שֹׁמְרֵ֣י הַ⁠בַּ֔יִת

"when the guards of the house will tremble"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s body as if it were a house and of the person’s arms, which protect the body, as if they were guards of the house. In old age the arms become weak and tremble. Alternate translation: [when your arms, which protect your body, will tremble]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing literal household guards who shake with weakness or fear in a time of sadness and decline. Alternate translation: [when the men who guard the house will shake]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִֽתְעַוְּת֖וּ אַנְשֵׁ֣י הֶ⁠חָ֑יִל

"and the men of valor will be bent over"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s legs or back as if they were men of valor, that is strong men. In old age the legs and back become weak and bent. Alternate translation: [and your legs and back, which were once strong, will become weak and bent]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing literal strong men who cower in a time of sadness and decline. Alternate translation: [and the strong warriors will cower]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:3 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בָטְל֤וּ הַ⁠טֹּֽחֲנוֹת֙ כִּ֣י מִעֵ֔טוּ

"and the women grinders cease because they are few"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s teeth as if they were women grinders who grind grain. In old age only a few teeth are left, so a person can no longer chew well. Alternate translation: [and your teeth stop chewing because only a few of them are left]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing literal women who grind grain and who stop working because only a few of them remain. Alternate translation: [and the women who grind grain stop working because there are only a few of them]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠חָשְׁכ֥וּ הָ⁠רֹא֖וֹת בָּ⁠אֲרֻבּֽוֹת

"and those who look at the window will grow dark"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s eyes as if they were people who look at the window. In old age the eyes grow dark, that is they no longer see well. Alternate translation: [and your eyes, which look out at the world, will grow dim]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing literal people looking out of windows who become gloomy in a time of sadness and decline. Alternate translation: [and the people who look out from the windows will become gloomy]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠סֻגְּר֤וּ דְלָתַ֨יִם֙ בַּ⁠שּׁ֔וּק

"and {the} doors will be shut in the street"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s ears or lips as if they were doors that are shut. In old age a person hears less of what happens in the street, or speaks less. Alternate translation: [and your ears will be closed to the sounds in the street]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing literal doors that open onto the street and that people shut in a time of sadness and decline. Alternate translation: [and people will shut the doors that open onto the street]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁפַ֖ל ק֣וֹל הַֽ⁠טַּחֲנָ֑ה

"when the sound of the grinding {is} low"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of an old person’s hearing becoming faint, so that even the sound of the grinding is low. Alternate translation: [when you can barely hear the sound of people grinding grain]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing the literal sound of a mill growing quiet because people are no longer grinding grain. Alternate translation: [when the sound of people grinding grain becomes quiet]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יָקוּם֙ לְ⁠ק֣וֹל הַ⁠צִּפּ֔וֹר

"and a person rises at the sound of the bird"

This could mean: (1) that the implication is that old people sleep lightly and wake up early, even at a small sound such as a bird singing. Alternate translation: [and a person wakes up early at even the small sound of a bird]; or (2) that the implication is that an old person’s voice becomes thin and high, so that it sounds like the voice of a bird. Alternate translation: [and a person’s voice becomes thin like the sound of a bird]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יִשַּׁ֖חוּ כָּל־בְּנ֥וֹת הַ⁠שִּֽׁיר

"and all the daughters of song are stooped"

Here, daughters of song refers either to songs or to singers. This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of songs as if they were women who are stooped, that is bowed down low. In old age a person’s singing voice becomes weak, or the person can no longer hear songs well. Alternate translation: [and your voice will become too weak to sing any song]; or (2) that Qoheleth is describing singers who bow down in grief in a time of sadness and decline. Alternate translation: [and all the women who sing will bow down in grief]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠יִשַּׁ֖חוּ כָּל־בְּנ֥וֹת הַ⁠שִּֽׁיר

"and all the daughters of song are stooped"

The expression are stooped is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and all the daughters of song bow down low]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠גָּבֹ֤הַּ יִרָ֨אוּ֙ וְ⁠חַתְחַתִּ֣ים בַּ⁠דֶּ֔רֶךְ

"they are afraid of a high {thing} and terrors {are} in the way"

The implication is that old people are afraid of climbing up to a high thing and are afraid of the dangers they might meet when they walk outside, so that terrors are in the way. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [old people are afraid of climbing up to a high place, and they fear dangers when they walk outside]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יָנֵ֤אץ הַ⁠שָּׁקֵד֙

"and the almond tree blossoms"

Qoheleth is speaking as if the white hair of an old person were the almond tree that blossoms. He means that, as an almond tree becomes covered with white blossoms, an old person’s hair turns white. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their hair turns white]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יִסְתַּבֵּ֣ל הֶֽ⁠חָגָ֔ב

"and the locust moves along"

This could mean: (1) that Qoheleth is speaking of an old person as if he were the locust that drags itself along slowly. In old age a person walks stiffly and with difficulty. Alternate translation: [and the old person drags himself along like a locust that can barely move], or (2) that even something as light as a locust becomes a burden to an old person. Alternate translation: [and even a locust becomes a heavy burden]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠תָפֵ֖ר הָֽ⁠אֲבִיּוֹנָ֑ה

"and the caper-fruit fails"

Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s desire were the caper-fruit, which people ate in order to increase their appetite. He means that in old age a person no longer desires food or other pleasures, just as the caper-fruit can fail to make a person hungry. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a person no longer desires food or other pleasures]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 (#5)
content:
הֹלֵ֤ךְ & אֶל־בֵּ֣ית עוֹלָמ֔⁠וֹ

"is going to his eternal home"

Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase is going to his eternal home. The eternal home is the grave, where a person’s body stays forever. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [is going to die]

See: Euphemism

title: Ecclesiastes 12:6 (#1)
content:
ירחק חֶ֣בֶל הַ⁠כֶּ֔סֶף וְ⁠תָרֻ֖ץ גֻּלַּ֣ת הַ⁠זָּהָ֑ב

"the cord of silver is removed and the bowl of gold is broken"

Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s life were a lamp, a bowl of gold that hangs on a cord of silver. He means that just as the lamp falls and breaks when the cord is removed, a person’s life ends when he dies. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person dies, just as a lamp falls and breaks when its cord is removed]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:6 (#2)
content:
ירחק

"is removed"

The phrase is removed is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is however a correction, “is snapped,” in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. This correction fits well with the image of a cord that breaks and lets a lamp fall. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [is snapped]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Ecclesiastes 12:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠תִשָּׁ֤בֶר כַּד֙ עַל־הַ⁠מַּבּ֔וּעַ וְ⁠נָרֹ֥ץ הַ⁠גַּלְגַּ֖ל אֶל־הַ⁠בּֽוֹר

"and the pitcher is shattered at the fountain and the wheel is crushed at the cistern"

Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s life were the pitcher that people use to draw water at the fountain and the wheel that people use to lift water at the cistern. He means that just as these things can no longer bring up water once they are broken, a person’s life ends when he dies. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a person’s life comes to an end the way a broken pitcher and a crushed wheel can no longer draw up water]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠תִשָּׁ֤בֶר כַּד֙ עַל־הַ⁠מַּבּ֔וּעַ וְ⁠נָרֹ֥ץ הַ⁠גַּלְגַּ֖ל אֶל־הַ⁠בּֽוֹר

"and the pitcher is shattered at the fountain and the wheel is crushed at the cistern"

The expressions is shattered and is crushed are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the pitcher shatters at the fountain, and the wheel breaks apart at the cistern]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֧ב הֶ⁠עָפָ֛ר עַל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ כְּ⁠שֶׁ⁠הָיָ֑ה

"and the dust returns to the earth as that it was"

Here, the dust represents the body which God formed from dust. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the body returns to the earth as the dust that it was]

See: Metonymy

title: Ecclesiastes 12:8 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠קּוֹהֶ֖לֶת

"the Qoheleth"

See how you translated this name in 1:1.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Ecclesiastes 12:8 (#2)
content:
הֲבֵ֧ל הֲבָלִ֛ים

"Vapor of vapors"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:2.

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 12:8 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠כֹּ֥ל הָֽבֶל

"Everything {is} vapor"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:2.

See: Hyperbole

title: Ecclesiastes 12:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יֹתֵ֕ר שֶׁ⁠הָיָ֥ה קֹהֶ֖לֶת חָכָ֑ם ע֗וֹד לִמַּד

"More {than} that Qoheleth was wise, again he taught"

The phrase More than that means “in addition to the fact that.” The author is saying that besides the fact that Qoheleth was wise, he also taught the people knowledge. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In addition to being wise, Qoheleth also taught]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Ecclesiastes 12:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אִזֵּ֣ן וְ⁠חִקֵּ֔ר תִּקֵּ֖ן מְשָׁלִ֥ים הַרְבֵּֽה

"and he weighed and he searched. He ordered many proverbs"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Here, weighed means “carefully evaluated.” Alternate translation: [and he carefully evaluated proverbs, and he searched them out and set them in order]

See: Ellipsis

title: Ecclesiastes 12:10 (#1)
content:
דִּבְרֵי־חֵ֑פֶץ

"words of pleasure"

The author is using the possessive form to describe words that are characterized by pleasure, that is, words that are pleasing or fitting. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [pleasing words]

See: Possession

title: Ecclesiastes 12:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָת֥וּב & דִּבְרֵ֥י אֱמֶֽת

"and words of truth were written"

The expression were written is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that Qoheleth was the one who wrote these words. Alternate translation: [and he wrote words of truth]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:10 (#3)
content:
דִּבְרֵ֥י אֱמֶֽת

"words of truth"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of truth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [words that are true]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#1)
content:
דִּבְרֵ֤י חֲכָמִים֙ כַּ⁠דָּ֣רְבֹנ֔וֹת

"The} words of wise {people are} like goads"

The point of this comparison is that just as goads are pointed sticks that prod cattle to move in the right direction, so the words of wise people prod people to think and live in the right way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The words of wise people prod people to think and live in the right way, as goads prod cattle to move in the right direction]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#2)
content:
וּֽ⁠כְ⁠מַשְׂמְר֥וֹת נְטוּעִ֖ים

"and like nails implanted"

The point of this comparison is that just as nails that someone has driven firmly into wood stay fixed in place, so the collected sayings of wise people are firm and lasting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and as firm and lasting as nails driven deeply into wood]

See: Simile

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#3)
content:
וּֽ⁠כְ⁠מַשְׂמְר֥וֹת נְטוּעִ֖ים

"and like nails implanted"

The expression implanted is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and like nails that someone has driven in firmly]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#4)
content:
בַּעֲלֵ֣י אֲסֻפּ֑וֹת

"are} masters of collections"

The author is using masters of collections as a common expression of the culture. This could mean: (1) that the expression refers to the collected sayings of wise people. Alternate translation: [are the collected sayings of wise people]; or (2) that the expression refers to the people who collect wise sayings. Alternate translation: [are those who collect wise sayings]

See: Idiom

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#5)
content:
נִתְּנ֖וּ מֵ⁠רֹעֶ֥ה אֶחָֽד

"They are given by one Shepherd"

The expression are given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [One Shepherd gives them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11 (#6)
content:
מֵ⁠רֹעֶ֥ה אֶחָֽד

"one Shepherd"

The author is speaking as if the one who gives wise sayings were a Shepherd who guides his sheep. This could mean: (1) that one Shepherd refers to God, who is the source of all wisdom and who guides his people as a shepherd guides sheep. Alternate translation: [God, who guides his people like a shepherd]; or (2) that the expression refers to a wise teacher or king who guides people with wise sayings. Alternate translation: [one wise teacher, who guides people like a shepherd]

See: Metaphor

title: Ecclesiastes 12:12 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠הֵ֖מָּה

"than them"

The pronoun them refers to the words of wise people mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [than the words of wise people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Ecclesiastes 12:12 (#2)
content:
בְּנִ֣⁠י

"my son"

Here the masculine term son has a generic sense that includes both men and women. The author is using it to address anyone who learns from him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [my student]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Ecclesiastes 12:12 (#3)
content:
הִזָּהֵ֑ר

"be warned"

The expression be warned is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I warn you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Ecclesiastes 12:12 (#4)
content:
יְגִעַ֥ת בָּשָֽׂר

"is} weariness of flesh"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of weariness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [makes the body very tired]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Ecclesiastes 12:13 (#1)
content:
זֶ֖ה כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָֽם

"this is the whole of humanity"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. This could mean: (1) that the author means that fearing God and keeping his commandments is the whole duty of every person. Alternate translation: [this is the whole duty of every person]; or (2) that the author means that this is what every person was created for. Alternate translation: [this is what every person was made for]; or (3) that the author means that this applies to every person. Alternate translation: [this applies to every person]

See: Ellipsis

"everything hidden"

The expression hidden is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The context indicates that people have hidden these things. Alternate translation: [everything that people have hidden]

"whether good or whether evil"

The author is referring to all of the things that people do by naming two major components, good and evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [no matter what kind of deed it is]
